items.body:
Canada’s much-anticipated summit with the European Union began Thursday after months of speculation around how a new alliance between the two bodies will take shape.

On the first day of the two-day summit in Montreal, Prime Minister Mark Carney and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Canada and the EU would collaborate on AI and both used the term “associate member” when referring to how the two sides will strengthen ties.

Von der Leyen made headlines last month when she publicly invited Carney to grow the Canada-EU relationship and first floated the term “associate member” in a speech. Some countries have pushed back on that label, and Canadian officials have called the partnership an “alliance for the future.”

Carney has pushed for closer ties with global partners while Ottawa and Washington spar in a trade war that has dragged on throughout U.S. President Donald Trump’s term.

items.title: Binance’s possible hack triggers US$3 billion freeze in crypto assets
items.description: Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, said on Thursday it had frozen US$3 billion in crypto assets as it investigated a potential security breach, with stablecoin issuers Circle and Tether freezing related assets.

items._ogDesc: Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, said on Thursday it had frozen US$3 billion in crypto assets as it investigated a potential security breach, with stablecoin issuers Circle and Tether freezing related assets.
items.body:
Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, said on Thursday it had frozen US$3 billion in crypto assets as it investigated a potential security breach, with stablecoin issuers Circle and Tether freezing related assets.

“Binance will cover all hacking losses,” Binance co-founder Yi He said, without providing more details about the incident.

The market impact of the possible hacking, which could be the largest-ever crypto heist according to analytics firm Chainalysis, was felt immediately in early Asian trading on Friday.

Bitcoin dropped about two per cent to a six-week low of US$77,646 and ether fell around two per cent to a two-month low of US$2,238.76.

BNB, a token originally launched as Binance Coin that can be used to pay Binance fees, was down more than eight per cent over the past 24 hours at US$694, according to market aggregator CoinGecko.

Crypto exchange Coinbase Global slid 4.8 per cent while those of bitcoin buyer Strategy fell nearly six per cent in extended U.S. trading.

Binance said the amount frozen could increase as it worked with law enforcement agencies, token issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and other industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets.

Binance co-founder Changpeng Zhao, who no longer runs the company, said in a post on X that the incident “looked like a hack.”

Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has more than 335 million registered users globally and had about US$160 billion in assets under custody as of the exchange’s 2024 annual report.

Binance has secure asset fund

Binance runs a secure asset fund for users, according to its website, which is a reserve held entirely in bitcoin that is intended to protect user assets in cases of security breaches.

“It’s becoming very hard to counter hacks as AI can find vulnerabilities faster than you can fix them, said Bernardo Brites, CEO of Trace Finance, a payments and stablecoin infrastructure company.

“My view is that users will move away from smaller and medium-sized exchanges, (it is) becoming too risky to park your money somewhere that couldn’t cover a hack of meaningful size.”

Tether said it had frozen nearly US$1.57 billion in assets linked to the incident, while Circle froze more than US$800 million.

Binance said it was conducting security checks and would resume withdrawals once the issue was fully resolved. It added user funds remained safe and that teams were reviewing the incident.

The exchange also temporarily suspended trading on its Binance Alpha platform as a precaution. World Liberty Financial, a crypto company linked to U.S. President Donald Trump and his family, said on Thursday it had worked with cryptocurrency custodian BitGo to freeze funds stolen in what it described as a Binance hack. Binance’s Yi said US$27 million in stablecoins and about US$2 million worth of World Liberty tokens had been frozen.

Crypto firm Ripple also froze roughly US$200 million in funds, Yi said. Jack McDonald, senior vice-president of stablecoins at Ripple, said the company was closely monitoring reports of a potential exploit involving Binance and was freezing affected funds and coordinating with relevant parties.

Incident adds to string of crypto thefts

Miguel Morel, CEO of blockchain intelligence firm Arkham, said data indicated that billions of dollars appeared to have been hacked from Binance by an unknown actor, though the exact cause had not been confirmed. Morel said the incident began around 4:30 p.m. EDT (2030 GMT) and appeared to be ongoing.

The incident adds to a string of crypto thefts. Last year, attackers stole US$2.9 billion worth of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 attacks, according to researchers at TRM Labs. In September, cryptocurrency exchange Bitget said roughly US$350 million in crypto had been stolen from its platform, underscoring the industry’s vulnerability to hackers.

Authorities have warned that organized crime groups are increasingly using cryptocurrencies to move funds across borders outside the traditional financial system.

Binance.US, a separate cryptocurrency exchange, said it was not affected by the security incident.

Coinbase said it was unaffected and was monitoring the situation.

In an unrelated incident earlier on Thursday, prediction market operator Polymarket temporarily halted trading after a security incident involving a third-party provider. It later resumed trading and said it would fully reimburse affected traders.

(Reporting by Tom Westbrook and Ankur Banerjee in Singapore, Vallari Srivastava and Anusha Shah in Bengaluru and Mrinmay Dey in Mexico City; Writing by Scott Murdoch; Editing by Michelle Price, Sherry Jacob-Phillips and Jamie Freed)

items.title: Proposed Air Canada-United arrangement would cost customers millions: watchdog
items.description: The federal Competition Bureau says that a proposed Air Canada and United Airlines arrangement could harm competition on 10 routes between Canada and the U.S., costing consumers millions of dollars in airfare.

items._ogDesc: The federal Competition Bureau says that a proposed Air Canada and United Airlines arrangement could harm competition on 10 routes between Canada and the U.S., costing consumers millions of dollars in airfare.
items.body:
The federal Competition Bureau says that a proposed Air Canada and United Airlines arrangement could harm competition on 10 routes between Canada and the U.S., costing consumers millions of dollars in airfare.

The watchdog report was sent to Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon for review.

The 10 affected routes connect Toronto, Montreal, Ottawa and Vancouver with Chicago, Cleveland, Denver, Houston, New York, San Francisco and Washington.

The routes proposed are restricted by a 2012 consent agreement.

“The restrictions were put in place after the Bureau concluded that similar coordination between the airlines would substantially harm competition. The restrictions remain in force today,” the Competition Bureau said in a news release.

“The Bureau found that the proposed arrangement would eliminate an important source of competition between the airlines on these routes.”

The Canadian and American airlines account for all non-stop traffic on five of the 10 routes, the Bureau said, and have “significant combined market shares on the others.”

Transport Canada says the two airlines have operated under the Transborder Joint Business Arrangement (TBJBA), which allows them to work together on certain routes, since 2022.

“This includes coordination on joint pricing, inventory management, revenue sharing, and the exchange of competitively sensitive information,” Competition Bureau Canada said.

The airlines’ newly proposed arrangement includes an amended and restated version, which the Bureau said would “eliminate competition” on the 10 routes currently restricted.

“If the (agreement) is successfully rescinded, this would permit the Parties to coordinate on the (10) routes in the same manner contemplated by the TBJBA,” the Bureau said.

The proposed expansion would likely mean higher prices and “millions of dollars in consumer harm each year,” it stated, as the Air Canada-United arrangement could create monopoly or near-monopoly conditions on several routes.

“Competition between airlines helps keep fares lower and gives travellers more choice and better service,” said interim commissioner Jeanne Pratt.

“Our review found that allowing Air Canada and United to coordinate on these routes would likely reduce competition on key Canada-U.S. routes and lead to higher prices for travellers.”

items._ogDesc: Air Canada has lowered its earnings outlook by hundreds of millions of dollars for the year thanks to sky-high fuel costs after a tough quarter that saw its bottom line nearly cut in half.
items.body:
Sky-high fuel costs pushed Air Canada to slash its profit forecast by hundreds of millions of dollars for the year after a turbulent quarter that saw its bottom line nearly cut in half.

The country’s largest airline recovered less than half of its fuel expanse last quarter, but aims to recoup about 70 per cent in the current one, said chief financial officer John Di Bert.

The surging price of kerosene, particularly in September and after, drove a year-over-year fuel cost increase of 75 per cent or $906 million in the three months ended Sept. 30, he said.

Amid an ongoing conflict in the Middle East that has throttled global oil exports, Di Bert expects the fuel price to hover around $1.72 per litre — “significantly higher than originally planned.”

“That is with us for at least the foreseeable future,” he said.

As a result, passengers can expect more ticket price hikes.

“Fare increases remain the primary tool to offset a higher fuel environment,” he said.

Airfares in Canada rose 19.4 per cent year-over-year in September, according to Statistics Canada.

Air Canada lowered its 2026 financial outlook on Thursday, forecasting between $2.4 billion and $2.7 billion in earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, versus the $2.9 billion to $3.2 billion it predicted less than three months ago.

The revision comes after its net income attributable to shareholders fell 47 per cent to $139 million year-over-year in its latest quarter.

However, operating revenues jumped 21 per cent to a third-quarter record of $6.98 billion, as the Montreal-based company ratcheted up airfares.

The financial clouds on the near horizon relate partly to the lag between bookings and fuel prices, said chief commercial officer Mark Galardo.

Air Canada has a much higher proportion of long-haul to short-haul flights than its U.S. competitors. Those longer trips are generally booked further in advance, at prices that reflect the fuel price expectations at that time.

“Once those bookings are in, it’s hard to recapture (fuel costs),” Galardo noted.

National Bank analyst Cameron Doerksen said that while the timeline to full cost recovery “has been pushed to the right,” complete recuperation would be possible in the first half of next year.

“We believe that higher fuel costs are weighing more heavily on the profitability of Air Canada’s competitors, which ultimately will lead to more industry capacity cuts to the benefit of Air Canada,” he said in a note to investors.

The sustained decline in demand for travel to the United States has pushed the carrier to scale back its cross-border service. Earlier this year, it halted or delayed eight transborder routes for the fall, then cut four more routes planned for this summer.

Canadians’ return trips by air from the United States numbered 23 per cent fewer in August than the same month two years earlier, according to Statistics Canada.

In the same period, Air Canada flight volumes between the two countries fell 13 per cent, figures from aviation data tracker Cirium show.

However, Galardo has cautioned against reading too much into cuts to some of its cross-border corridors, noting several routes had been added as well.

He said the strength of the U.S. dollar, higher profit margins south of the border and growing American demand for trips to Canada all provide tailwinds. Air Canada is also seeking to leverage the country’s location as a stopover point for Europeans and North and South Americans who cross the Atlantic Ocean.

“I’ve got no reason to be concerned about the state of the transborder market,” Galardo said.

Air Canada has embarked on a major expansion of its network overseas, announcing last month seven new routes in Europe and Asia for next summer.

Driving the expansion are new long-range Airbus A321 single-aisle jets as well as Boeing 787 wide-bodies, though major delivery delays have hampered their rollout.

The first of an expected 30 Airbus A321XLRs arrived at Air Canada in April. Six more of the fuel-efficient single-aisle aircraft  — many bound for transatlantic service — are set for delivery this quarter. Its first two 787-10s are due before the end of the year as well, on top of seven Airbus A220s — smaller narrow-bodies assembled north of Montreal — Di Bert said.

The A321s jets burn 15 to 20 per cent less fuel than wide-body planes on trips across the Atlantic, he said. “This is meaningful in any environment, but it matters even more in this current fuel environment.”

On an adjusted basis, the company’s adjusted earnings stayed flat at 75 cents per share last quarter, well above analysts’ predictions of 50 cents per share, according to financial markets firm LSEG Data & Analytics.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 29, 2026.

Christopher Reynolds, The Canadian Press

items.title: Children especially vulnerable to climate change, expert witness says
items.description: A child psychiatrist and pediatrician has described how children are disproportionately vulnerable to the effects of climate change in her testimony at Canada’s first youth-led climate trial.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Plaintiffs from the La Rose v. His Majesty the King court case rally in Vancouver, on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Ethan Cairns]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">ETHAN CAIRNS</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: A child psychiatrist and pediatrician has described how children are disproportionately vulnerable to the effects of climate change in her testimony at Canada’s first youth-led climate trial.
items.body:
A child psychiatrist and pediatrician has described how children are disproportionately vulnerable to the effects of climate change in her testimony at Canada’s first youth-led climate trial.

Dr. Elizabeth Pinsky outlined to Federal Court in Vancouver an array of risks, from susceptibility to extreme heat, air pollution and tick-borne illness to anxiety and depression linked to climate change.

The Boston-based doctor pointed to several physiological factors, testifying that babies and very young children have immature thermoregulatory systems, diminishing their ability to regulate their internal temperature in a heat wave.

Children breathe more rapidly than adults and take in more air pollution relative to their size, said Pinsky, an assistant professor at Harvard Medical School.

There is also a “temporal reality,” she said, as younger people are “simply at increased risk” from climate hazards over the course of their lifetimes.

As climate change worsens, so too will the health harms, she testified on Thursday.

“There’s just no question left in the medical literature about whether that’s true.”

Pinsky is a witness for 15 young plaintiffs in the trial in Federal Court in Vancouver, where they’re arguing that federal legislation violates their constitutional rights by continuing Canada’s trajectory of greenhouse gas emissions.

She described the knowledge that “the people who should be protecting you and keeping you safe and safeguarding your future are not just failing to do so, but knowingly failing to do so” as a unique harm among children.

The plaintiffs’ lawyer, Catherine Boies Parker, told the court in her opening statement on Monday that the case was not about the existence of climate change. 

Rather, it hinges on whether the government is “constitutionally required to stop making it worse,” she said.

“The plaintiffs are asking this court to hold Canada legally accountable for its role in continuing and worsening the climate crisis that is causing harm.”

Pinsky also described some of the mental health effects of climate change among young people, including “eco-anxiety,” saying it can include feelings of fear, sadness, grief, anger, and a sense of betrayal and powerlessness.

She explained the term “solastalgia,” meaning “the experience of feeling homesick when you are at home, but home has changed around you.”

Someone might feel a sense of solastalgia when their childhood home is now engulfed in wildfire smoke every summer, Pinsky said.

Nothing could fully protect children from climate harms other than ceasing to burn fossil fuels and halting climate change, she said.

Pinsky is set to be cross-examined by Ottawa’s lawyers on Friday.

Earlier Thursday, the court heard from Stanford University professor Mark Jacobson, an expert in environmental engineering and atmospheric science, who said it is “definitely” possible for Canada to shift to full renewable energy by 2050.

He said the transition is technically and economically feasible, and the obstacles on that course are social and political in nature.

Jacobson has developed sophisticated models and road maps to help cities, states and countries, including Canada, make the shift to renewable energy.

Canada does not need to rely on fossil fuels, he said, outlining how the country could meet its energy demands by tapping “humongous” resources and opportunities in wind, solar and geothermal, along with pre-existing hydroelectric capacity.

Combine that with the electrification of energy and transportation and “Canada can do it,” Jacobson said of transitioning to renewables by mid-century.

“Whether it actually does it by 2050 is more of a social and political question.”

Jacobson said electricity is significantly more efficient than combustion.

“By electrifying everything and providing that electricity from renewables, you use a huge amount less energy. In Canada, it’s like 60 per cent less energy,” he said.

The shift would also slash air pollution and emissions that cause global heating, he said, noting thousands of people die every year from air pollution in Canada.

Jacobson agreed under cross-examination by a lawyer for the federal government that his report prepared for the trial did not present any policy proposals for Ottawa.

He also acknowledged the study did not account for potential “bottlenecks” in Canada’s renewable transition, such as supply-chain constraints.

Jacobson had testified earlier Thursday that his study projected a net job loss for Canada in the shift to renewables, though it wasn’t a comprehensive account.

The figure excluded “the jobs that would be involved in the production of electric vehicles, electric heat pumps, other electric appliances and machines, and also some transmission distribution jobs,” he said under cross-examination.

This report by Brenna Owen, The Canadian Press, was first published Oct. 29, 2026.

items._ogDesc: Prime Minister Mark Carney says his government will invest up to $1.6 billion in Canadian AI company Cohere.
items.body:
OTTAWA -- Prime Minister Mark Carney said Thursday his government will invest up to $1.6 billion in Canadian AI company Cohere.

He made the announcement in Montreal as he welcomed European Union leaders to a summit aimed at forging closer ties.

“We are not waiting for the future of AI to be decided somewhere else by those we don’t know or by whom we don’t trust. We’re building it right here in the right way,” Carney said.

In April, Cohere announced it would merge with Germany’s Aleph Alpha and said the company would be “anchored in” Germany and Canada.

On Thursday, Carney called the partnership a concrete example of what Canada and Europe can build together.

He also said that, under the agreement, Cohere will stay Canadian.

Carney said the government is making the announcement on “a commercial basis, alongside private investors including Nvidia, Bell, and Germany’s Schwarz Group.”

Cohere CEO Aidan Gomez said at the announcement that the company, which was founded seven years ago, is now “one of the very few companies in the world building frontier AI technology at a global scale.”

He added that it’s the largest AI company outside the U.S. and China.

In a press release issued Thursday, the government said the funding would be provided in stages, with regular reporting on commitments made by the company.

Those commitments include creating at least 1,000 “new high-paying Canadian technical jobs” and committing at least $1.7 billion to building more computing infrastructure by 2030.

The government says Cohere will also maintain its Canadian headquarters and incorporation, invest in research partnerships, create opportunities for students and graduates and continue working with the Canadian AI Safety Institute.

“Cohere will now be able to develop far more advanced models and products, scale up its computing infrastructure, and expand its Canadian workforce to serve more businesses and governments in Canada and around the world,” the press release said.

“Building this capability at home ultimately means that Canadian businesses and governments will have more choice in how they adopt AI and greater control over their sensitive information.”

In 2024, the government announced it would provide up to $240 million to Cohere to boost its computing capacity. In 2025, Ottawa signed an agreement with the company to identify areas where AI can enhance public service operations.

Artificial Intelligence Minister Evan Solomon has often pointed to Cohere as an element of Canada’s strength in AI, saying Canada is one of only a few countries around the world with a large language model.

items.title: Online competition helped close his last shop. Now he’s giving retail another shot
items.description: While many small business owners across Canada are considering getting out brick-and-mortar retail amid rising costs and uncertainty, Craig Enman is getting back to in-person sales on P.E.I.

items._ogDesc: While many small business owners across Canada are considering getting out brick-and-mortar retail amid rising costs and uncertainty, Craig Enman is getting back to in-person sales on P.E.I.
items.body:
CHARLOTTETOWN – While many small business owners across Canada are considering getting out brick-and-mortar retail amid rising costs and uncertainty, Craig Enman is getting back to in-person sales on P.E.I.

Enman opened Distinctive Decor’s Treasure Hut at Charlottetown’s Confederation Court Mall in August. It is not his first foray into running a storefront. For 15 years, he operated a silver and gemstone jewellery business with several locations in Nova Scotia. But navigating changing shopping habits and battling competition from major retailers such as Amazon and Walmart, led him to close it.

Still, he was not ready to give up on the industry.

“There’s always a risk,” Enman said. “It’s financial. It’s work. It’s a lot of effort. But this is what I wanted.”

Inside his new shop, shelves are lined with fine porcelain, crystal, one-of-a-kind antiques and collectibles. It’s a place built for browsing and discovering the beauty of the past.

But Enman acknowledges the present is not an easy time for entrepreneurs.

“Cost of living is on everybody’s mind,” he said. “But it’s also the uncertainty in the marketplace. The Canada-U.S. relationship isn’t going the best.”

Trade tensions and expenses lead to closures

According to estimates released Thursday by Statistics Canada, the number of active businesses on P.E.I. dipped slightly, from 4,195 in June to 4,182 in July. Openings fell from 228 to 217, while closures rose from 218 to 226.

A similar pattern played out nationally. The number of active businesses across Canada declined by 400 to 937,821. Openings fell by 1,444, while closures edged up by 106.

The figures offer a snapshot of July rather than current conditions, but the Canadian Federation of Independent Business (CFIB) says they fit into a longer-running trend. Since early 2024, more businesses have been exiting the Canadian market than entering it, which the organization describes as an “entrepreneurial drought.”

CFIB’s Atlantic director Frederic Gionet says a combination of trade tensions, volatile energy prices and mounting expenses is making people think twice about starting a new venture.

“The cost of doing business is very high,” he said.

‘Cost of business has gone up’

Gionet adds that for brick-and-mortar retailers, the expenses do not stop at stocking the shelves. Commercial property taxes can be two to three times higher than residential rates for properties of comparable value in parts of the region, he said. For some of the smallest businesses, that bill can account for more than 10 per cent of operating expenses.

Meanwhile, costs associated with permits, licences and labour continue to put pressure on owners.

“So they have to pass these costs down to consumers, who in turn are tightening their belts themselves,” Gionet said.

And while there has been a strong push to shop local in recent years, he says finding the best deal can ultimately dictate where people spend their money.

The financial fallout of the pandemic is lingering as well. Gionet says many owners have not had time to fully recover.

“The cost of living has gone up substantially and the cost of business has gone up substantially,” he said, noting the compounding effect of the last few years.

Some are deciding they have had enough.

A CFIB report released Oct. 22 found that 63 per cent of Canadian small business owners plan to end their business within the next decade. Retirement is the leading reason, cited by 78 per cent, while 21 per cent identified burnout or stress and 20 per cent pointed to high operating costs.

But for Enman, who is also an architectural technologist, the shop is his retirement plan. He is spending his days surrounded by craftsmanship and artwork he admires, and sales have been steady.

“I’m very happy,” he said.

The post Canada’s Housing Agency Forecasts Surge In Mortgage Arrears, But It May Be Worse appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: The CMHC forecasts Canadian mortgage arrears will hit a 9-year high by 2027. Here is why the national housing agency might be underestimating the fallout.
items.body:
Canada’s national housing agency is bearish on real estate over the near term. The CMHC’s latest forecast shows Canadian Bankers Association (CBA) mortgage arrears climbing into 2027. The trend is driven almost entirely by a surge in Ontario. That suggests they might be underestimating the fallout, since home prices in other provinces are only just starting to correct.

Canadian Mortgage Arrears Have Climbed Aggressively

The arrears rate at Canada’s banks is on an aggressive climb. The share of mortgages in arrears hit 0.29% in July, up 6 basis points (bps) from last year. That’s the highest rate since 2015, more than doubling from the record low less than 5 years ago. It isn’t over either.

Canadian Mortgage Arrears Forecast To Keep Climbing

Canadian mortgage arrears rate (90 days past due) and CMHC forecast.

Source: CBA; CMHC; Better Dwelling.

The CMHC forecasts the arrears rate will continue to rise through mid-2027. They expect it to hit 0.33% by February and hold there through June 2027, the end of the forecast period. That would push arrears to the highest level since 2012.

Why The CMHC Might Be Underestimating Arrears

A closer look at the forecast reveals the agency might be underestimating the stress. The projection is primarily driven by a 58% surge in arrears in Ontario, one of 2 provinces ending the forecast at a cycle high. Slow real estate sales, a rocky job market, and a price correction are cited as the drivers. However, they’re missing a key detail—other provinces haven’t seen a correction yet.

Canadian home prices made a substantial correction after most markets slipped in 2022. However, Ontario and BC are the only provinces to see a major correction, and only the former’s drop is bigger than the national average. Despite prices across the country getting a massive lift from the low-rate boom, all but 2 remain just off record highs. Slow sales are lingering as a result of market inefficiencies that still need to correct.

These provinces don’t appear to be immune to gravity, though. Last month, prices in regions that largely resisted the correction began making near-record declines. The declines have only just started in most of the country, potentially spreading Ontario’s climate to more markets. That would prove to be a major headwind for arrears in those regions.

items.title: ‘Immediately stop using’: Gas boilers, space heaters among latest recalls in Canada
items.description: Health Canada has announced recalls of residential gas boilers, children’s sensory swings and DREO space heaters over risks including carbon monoxide poisoning, falls and fires.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Health Canada latest trio of recalls include gas boilers, sensory swings and space heaters. (Health Canada)]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: Health Canada has announced recalls of residential gas boilers, children’s sensory swings and DREO space heaters over risks including carbon monoxide poisoning, falls and fires.
items.body:
Three products sold in Canada are being recalled following safety concerns also reported in the United States.

Health Canada issued consumer product recall notices for NTI- and HTP-brand residential gas boilers; Harkla children’s compression sensory swings and DREO portable space heaters on Thursday. Each of the companies mentioned in the recalls are offering free remedies, including repair kits, boiler upgrades and replacement heaters.

Consumers who own any of the affected products should stop “immediately stop using them,” according to each of the notices, and follow the companies’ instructions to obtain the appropriate remedy.

Gas boilers pose fire, carbon monoxide risks

Certain NTI and HTP residential gas boilers are being recalled because a component inside the units can crack during delayed ignition, allowing unburned gas to accumulate inside the sealed cabinet.

If the gas ignites, the boiler’s front cover can suddenly detach, creating a risk of serious injury or death from impact, fire or carbon monoxide poisoning.

The recall affects NTI boilers in the FTVN and TFTN series and HTP boilers in the EFTU series. The serial number is printed on the rating plate on the side of the boiler cabinet. Consumers should check the NTI safety recall page⁠ or the HTP safety notice page⁠ for the affected models and serial number ranges.

The products were sold from May 2021 to August 2025. About 2,261 affected units were sold in Canada and 4,726 in the United States.

As of Oct. 16, the company had received two incident reports and one injury report in Canada. It had received one incident report and no injury reports in the U.S. The company reported 34 total occurrences of the component breaking overall.

The recall said consumers should “immediately stop using” the recalled boilers and contact Ariston Canada Inc. for a free upgrade kit and help arranging installation by a certified technician.

“Consumers who must continue using the boiler while awaiting repair should have working smoke and carbon monoxide alarms in their homes,” the recall said.

Consumers can call 1-800-688-2575 for assistance or email email VCexchanger@ariston.com.

Harkla sensory swings recalled over fall hazard

Harkla children’s compression sensory swings are being recalled because the ceiling hook can separate from its mounting plate, potentially causing a child to fall and suffer serious injuries.

The recall covers blue compression sensory swings with a four-hole ceiling mounting plate and a drop length of 18 to 24 inches. The affected products are the Blue Compression Sensory Swing (SKU LS-COMP-1BLU) and Blue Compression Sensory Swing with Swivel (SKU LS-COMP-1BLU-SW).

The swings were sold from March 2020 to April 2025, with 5,534 sold in Canada and 25,541 in the United States.

As of Oct. 23, the company had received four reports of the hook separating from its mounting plate in Canada, including one injury report. In the U.S., it had received 29 reports of separation and 17 injury reports.

“Consumers should immediately stop using the recalled product and contact Harkla to obtain a repair kit,” the recall said.

The kit includes a replacement ceiling hook mounting plate, a safety strap and updated installation instructions. Consumers are also instructed to dispose of the original hooks according to municipal waste guidelines.

For assistance, call 844-442-7552, Monday to Friday, from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Pacific time, or email recall@harkla.co.

DREO space heaters recalled over overheating

DREO portable oscillating ceramic space heaters are being recalled because they can overheat and ignite, posing fire and burn hazards.

The recall affects model DR-HSH015, which are black heaters measuring about 29 centimetres wide, 33 centimetres tall and supplied with a remote control. The model number and manufacturing date appear on labels on the underside of the unit.

As of Oct. 22, the company had received one incident report and no injury reports in Canada. In the United States, it had received 16 incident reports, including one injury report.

TORONTO — Aecon Group Inc. reported a profit attributable to shareholders of $52.9 million during its third quarter, up from $40 million during the same period last year.

On a diluted per-share basis, the profit amounted to 74 cents, compared with 60 cents during the prior-year quarter.

The Toronto-based construction firm says revenue reached $1.92 billion during the period ended Sept. 30, rising year-over-year from $1.53 billion.

Aecon says its backlog hit a record of $14.56 billion, up from $10.78 billion a year earlier.

items.title: Ontario deficit grows to $16.9 billion as trade war with U.S. drags on
items.description: Ontario’s deficit has grown by more than $3 billion in the past few months as the province continues to face economic headwinds blowing up from the U.S.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Ontario Finance Minister Peter Bethlenfalvy delivers the government's fall economic statement in the legislature in Toronto, on Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Frank Gunn]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu"></media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Ontario’s deficit has grown by more than $3 billion in the past few months as the province continues to face economic headwinds blowing up from the U.S.
items.body:
Ontario’s deficit has grown by more than $3 billion in the past few months as the province continues to face economic headwinds blowing up from the U.S.

In an economic update delivered on Thursday, the Ford government said the deficit for 2026-27 is now projected to be $16.9 billion, up from the $13.8 billion that was projected in the budget tabled back in March.

“The impact of U.S. tariffs – which affect, among others, our steel, our auto and our manufacturing sectors – and global unrest impacting the price of gas has risen the cost of goods and has driven a sea of uncertainty,” Finance Minister Peter Bethlenfalvy said after delivering his fall economic statement. “As a result, Ontario families and businesses are feeling the impacts.”

However, he said the province has a plan “to protect workers, businesses and communities while building a stronger economy for the future,” despite the turbulence.

Most of the measures to do so have previously been announced. They include the joint $8.7 billion Canada-Ontario action plan with the federal government to bolster the steel, automotive and critical mineral sectors, as well as a recently announced plan to provide $8 billion in provincial tax relief to businesses by allowing them to write off a wide arrange of assets, another joint venture with the feds.

Some of the higher deficit owes to boosted funding to the government’s contingency and reserve funds, so-called rainy day funds.

Ontario has increased funding in its fiscal reserve fund from $1.5 billion to $2.2 billion. The province says the increase reflects “ongoing extraordinary circumstances, including significant trade-related risks to Ontario’s economic outlook.”

The province also topped up its contingency fund by an additional $3.8 billion in order to be prepared for further economic uncertainty, bringing the total in that fund to $4.9 billion.

Bethlenfalvy called the move “prudent” despite questions about whether it is worth going deeper into debt to add to those accounts.

“When we tabled the plan in March, we didn’t have Section 338 tariffs in place. These are the new tariffs that the president put on Canada. We didn’t have bans of certain products,” Bethlenfalvy told reporters.

“We had, based on best estimates from private sector economists, an economy that was growing at one per cent in Ontario. It’s (now) growing at 0.5 per cent because these tariffs are having an impact. We didn’t have a war in Iran. So, these are the types of things that are impacting our expenses. We don’t know exactly how they’re going to land in the next five months.”

Smaller deficits of $12.7 billion and $6.7 billion are expected over the next two fiscal years, with a small surplus of $200 million projected for 2029-30. The government had projected in the spring budget that it hoped to return to balance in 2028-29 with a surplus of $600 million.

The government says that, despite the economic uncertainty, the province’s economy is expected to continue growing. Real GDP is projected to increase by just 0.5 per cent in 2026 and 1.5 per cent in 2027.

Corporate tax up, personal income tax down

The higher deficit comes even as overall government revenue is actually up, now projected at $2 billion higher than the $232.6 billion forecast in the spring budget. The government says this is due to higher-than-expected federal transfers, as well as $878 million more in sales tax and around $1.5 billion more in corporate tax revenue.

At the same time, the province has seen revenue drop in other areas. Revenue from personal income tax is $1.7 billion less than previously forecast, due to less-than-expected revenue from the CRA for 2025. Government officials say this mainly reflects less capital gains tax revenue than expected and also stems from difficulties in projecting personal income revenue.

The province is also now projecting $3.28 billion in Land Transfer Tax revenue, $497 million less than forecasted in the budget. That’s mainly owing to the sluggish housing market, the government says.

Bethlenfalvy said he’s not concerned the province’s revenue are overly exposed to the slumping housing market.

To help make up the shortfall, the government is borrowing $3.9 billion more, bringing long-term borrowing to $51.1 billion.

U.S. tariffs impacting economy

The budget also lays out some details in terms of how the trade war has started to impact Ontario’s economy.

For example, steel exports to the U.S. totalled $4.1 billion in the first eight months of 2026. That compares to $8.4 billion over the same period in 2024, a drop of more than 50 per cent.

Auto exports to the U.S. over the same period declined 13.7 per cent from $39.9 billion to $34.5 billion.

While the government is projecting a return to balance in three years, a slower-growth scenario contemplates more large deficits over the next few years if, for example, the trade war drags on. A faster-growth scenario could see the province return to balance as soon as 2028-29 if it is resolved sooner.

Unemployment in the province sits at 7.2 per cent for 2026, but the government says it expects that to decrease to 6.1 per cent in 2029 with strengthening economic growth.

Opposition slams update

Responding to the government’s fall economic statement, opposition parties at Queen’s Park did not hold back.

“People simply cannot afford to live in this province,” Ontario Green Party Leader Mike Schreiner said.

He said the government should be looking at a wealth tax on the richest Ontarians in order to help balance the books.

Ontario NDP finance critic Jessica Bell also took aim at the update for failing to introduce any measures to help bring down the cost of living.

“Never have I seen a fall economic statement this mediocre,” Bell said. “I was shocked to see this fall economic statement does not do anything significant to address affordability. There are no significant measures in here to make it easier for people to pay for food at the grocery store or pay for rent at the end of the month.”

Interim Ontario Liberal Leader John Fraser said the update represents poor fiscal management more than economic conditions.

“The premier can’t keep blaming Trump. At some point, he’s got to look at his choices,” Fraser said.

Bethlenfalvy defended the update though, saying the government is already spending on a number of programs aimed at affordability, including a temporary break on HST off the purchase of a new home, as well as purpose-built rental buildings.

“These are a range of measures that are stimulating affordability for individuals, building for down the road, and keeping our construction sector jobs employed,” he said.

Other highlights

  • The province says it is increasing the penalty for people who fraudulently claim the first-time homebuyers’ credit
  • Ontario is capping the monthly credit for the Ontario Electricity Rebate at 1,200 KWh for residential customers as of May 1, 2027. The government says this will maintain affordability and ensure stability. The average residential customer uses 700KWh.
  • The $4 billion Protect Ontario Investment Fund announced in the spring budget has now been paused as the government explores possible better uses for the funds in the wake of further instability
  • The province is proposing narrowing the Ontario Computer Animation and Special Effects Tax Credit so that just TV and film producers will be eligible, a move asked for by the industry to help support it.

items.title: B.C. investors turn to retail plazas amid tight supply: report
items.description: Metro Vancouver retail vacancy falls below 1% in some areas: Re/Max
items._ogDesc: Metro Vancouver retail vacancy falls below 1% in some areas: Re/Max
items.body:
Neighbourhood retail vacancy has fallen below one per cent in some Metro Vancouver suburbs as investors turn to established properties, according to a new report.

The Re/Max Canada Fall 2026 Commercial Real Estate Report, released Thursday, found that retail vacancy had fallen below three per cent in downtown Vancouver and less than one per cent in some suburban neighbourhoods.

Conditions across B.C. remain uneven as some other markets, including Kelowna, has been more subdued with limited new building supply weighing on rental conditions and higher costs slowing development, the report said.

“Supply has become increasingly constrained in some of the country’s key commercial markets,” said Don Kottick, president of Re/Max Canada.

Commercial real estate investors in B.C. are favouring neighbourhood retail plazas and existing industrial properties, as demand for well-located space remains strong. Meanwhile, high construction and financing costs are weighing on new development, according to the report.

“We've seen considerable investment in established, income-producing properties this year, particularly in markets where demand remains strong,” said Kristie Kimnach, executive director of Re/Max Commercial, in a statement.

“The challenge in some of these markets seems to have been finding enough quality products to meet investor demand.”

Neighbourhood shopping plazas and grocery-anchored centres have attracted tenants in sectors including medical services, health, wellness, beauty and food services, the report said.

However, strong demand for industrial space has not necessarily translated into higher sale prices in Greater Vancouver. Industrial sale prices softened even as availability tightened, according to the report.

Kottick said the imbalance between strong demand for established retail space—particularly smaller units in high-demand markets—and a lack of new developments could persist amid higher bond yields and economic uncertainty.

Nationally, 11 of the 12 markets examined reported improving industrial market conditions, measured by increasing absorption and decreasing availability. Retail conditions improved in 10 markets, while multi-family improved in seven markets.

Looking ahead to 2027, Re/Max anticipates a gradual and uneven recovery in Canada's commercial real estate market.

“While demand for established, income-producing properties is expected to remain strong, limited new construction could create further supply challenges in markets where demand continues to grow,” the report said.

The report draws on data and insights from Re/Max brokers and agents across 12 major Canadian markets, comparing activity from January to June 2026 with the same period a year earlier.

items.title: Is homeownership becoming out of reach for young Canadians?
items.description: A new Zown survey maps the financial barriers standing between young Canadians and homeownership
items.content: <p>A new Zown survey maps the financial barriers standing between young Canadians and homeownership</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639288958170170403.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: A new Zown survey maps the financial barriers standing between young Canadians and homeownership
items.body:
For many young Canadians, the aspiration to own a home is not in doubt. What is increasingly uncertain is whether the financial foundations are there to support it.

A new survey puts those anxieties in sharp relief. Conducted by Toronto-based AI-powered real estate brokerage Zown and the Angus Reid Forum between October 14 and October 16, 2026, the 2026 Zown Homeownership & Financial Confidence Survey polled 1,500 adult Canadians.

It found that 82% of respondents aged 18 to 34 lacked confidence in at least one financial aspect of the homebuying process. That compares with 35% of those aged 35 to 54 and 50% of Canadians 55 and older who felt fully confident across the board.

Only 18% of those in the youngest cohort said they felt equipped to handle every financial dimension of a purchase.

Young buyers named saving and planning for a down payment (19%) and understanding ongoing ownership costs (19%) as the weakest points, followed by knowing how much home they could afford (18%), awareness of government incentives and programmes (14%), and calculating closing costs (10%).

Source: 2026 Zown Homeownership & Financial Confidence Survey — Zown / Angus Reid Forum — 1,500 adult Canadians — October 14–16, 2026 — margin of error ±2.53 percentage points, 19 times out of 20

Savings drawn down to meet everyday costs

Some 40% of Canadians dipped into long-term savings over the past year to cover ordinary expenses — 29% for emergencies, 22% for groceries and everyday purchases, and 13% for regular housing costs including rent or mortgage payments.

As Canadian Mortgage Professional’s reporting on Canada’s housing affordability challenges facing mortgage shoppers has shown, improving macro-level conditions in prices and rates have yet to relieve household-level financial strain.

Alberta led regionally at 48%, followed by Saskatchewan and Manitoba at 44% combined, Ontario and British Columbia at 41% each, Atlantic Canada at 35%, and Quebec at 34%.

“Housing affordability isn’t just about the price of a home. It’s also about whether Canadians can afford to become homeowners in the first place,” said Rishard Rameez, founder and chief executive officer of Zown, in Toronto.

“We’re asking people to save tens of thousands of dollars for a down payment when they’re already drawing on their savings to cover everyday expenses. That’s a fundamental challenge we can’t afford to overlook.”

Chris Allard of Smart Debt Mortgages says many borrowers are focusing on their personal finances and affordability rather than trying to predict the next twist in trade tensions or interest rates. https://t.co/lFVdypu2V5 — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 27, 2026

What brokers can offer underprepared clients

The confidence gap is steepest among those with no ownership history: only 13% of Canadians who have never owned a home but haven’t ruled it out say they feel prepared across all financial aspects, versus 46% of current homeowners.

Christa Tessier, broker and co-owner of Mortgage Advisors, previously told CMP that limited savings and elevated debt-to-income ratios are leaving many clients unable to qualify under standard lender requirements.

“Borrowers should focus on reducing debt as much as possible and maintaining good credit habits such as paying bills on time and keeping credit utilization low,” she said.

“Saving diligently for a down payment, closing costs, and a financial cushion can make a significant difference.”

Brokers who invest in that preparation work are starting to see results. Sarita Free, a mortgage agent with Mortgage Powered Financial Group in Norfolk County, Ontario, told CMP that 2025 and 2026 had been a turning point for buyers who had long been frozen out.

“A lot of my clients are first-time homebuyers and they’ve finally been able to break in,” she said.

“This year, I’m finding that they’re finally able to get into the market. With the 30-year amortization that we can now go to, I find a lot of my buyers that have been on the sidelines are finally able to… stay in their hometown where they’ve grown up, and not have to go elsewhere.”

items._ogDesc: Ontario mortgage arrears are nearing 2008 levels, with Toronto leading the stress. CMHC expects arrears to keep rising through mid-2027.
items.body:
The Ontario real estate downturn is expected to worsen. Mortgage arrears in the province are approaching 2008 levels, according to the CMHC. The risk is even further amplified in Greater Toronto, especially with private lenders. The agency warns Ontario’s sharpest and most persistent surge in arrears will persist through mid-2027.

Ontario’s Real Estate Boom and Bust

Ontario was the center of Canada’s real estate bubble and now it’s the center of its bust. The low rate frenzy sent prices 64% (+$393.6k) higher between April 2020 and March 2022. Since then, prices have dropped 26.7% (-$268.8k), reversing most gains—but not all. That little nugget is important when it comes to making sense of the arrears data we’ll get to soon. But first, let’s make sure we’re all on the same page when it comes to mortgage arrears.

The industry tends to frame rising arrears as a hard-hit consumer problem. In reality, households are hard hit during good times too. When someone can’t pay their mortgage, they typically try to sell. In a market boom, they sell pretty fast and feel like a genius when those profits flow in. When there’s a downturn, it takes longer to sell and not doing it fast enough means they end up in arrears. However, every property has a buyer—it’s a matter of price.

Would you rather go into arrears or lower your price? Obviously, the latter, which suggests those who don’t can’t actually do that. That’s mostly peak buyers, who in many cases see their equity wiped out entirely, and have to pay to sell. Ontario’s boom and bust is concentrated around investor-dominated Greater Toronto. CMHC doesn’t break down arrears by investors versus owner-occupiers, but the US housing crash provides some insight. Their downturn during the financial crisis is often blamed on overleveraged households, but the data shows it was an investor crash. Investors were just tapping subprime lenders to get more leverage.

Now that we have clear, let’s talk about arrears.

Ontario Mortgage Stress Builds, Private Lender Arrears Surge

Residential mortgage arrears rate at mortgage investment entities (MIEs): Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area (GTHA) vs Rest of Canada.

Source: CMHC; Better Dwelling.

Ontario has seen a surge in mortgage arrears. The arrears rate at CBA member banks hit 0.32% in Q2 2026, up 52% from a year before and over 5x the low in Q2 2022. The downturn is concentrated in the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area (GTHA) and Southwestern Ontario, says the CMHC.

CBA data understates the scale of the problem since it excludes roughly 1 in 5 mortgages. As previously noted, banks tend to sell or not renew underperforming or riskier loans. Those borrowers often end up at mortgage investment entities (MIEs), along with a clientele that can’t obtain traditional financing. MIEs have seen the arrears rate explode around the GTHA from 3.0% in Q3 2023 to 11.1% in Q1 2026. These lenders represent only 1.8% of outstanding mortgage balances nationally, but their GTHA arrears rate is over three times the national rate.

“Although MIEs account for a small share of the mortgage market, GTHA MIE arrears could provide an early signal of broader mortgage market stress,” explains the CMHC.

Ontario Mortgage Arrears Forecast To Rise Through Mid-2027

Ontario CBA mortgage arrears rate and CMHC forecast.

Source: CBA; CMHC; Better Dwelling.

The worst is yet to come, according to the CMHC. Even after the renewal shock, the agency expects a further erosion in credit quality in the province. They warn that the arrears rate in Ontario is expected to climb through mid-2027, with Toronto being primarily exposed.

“Ontario is projected to record the largest and most sustained increase in mortgage arrears, concentrated in the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area (GTHA) and Southwestern Ontario,” warns the CMHC.

Ontario isn’t alone in the potential worsening, but high prices and a concentration of trade tensions increase sensitivity. The agency specifically cites trade tensions threatening manufacturing employment, while weak resale conditions make it harder for stressed borrowers to exit.

items.content: <p>The 2026 Canadian Mortgage Awards arrive November 25 with 23 categories and a milestone to mark</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639288966737284341.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: The 2026 Canadian Mortgage Awards arrive November 25 with 23 categories and a milestone to mark
items.body:
On November 25, hundreds of Canada's mortgage brokers, lenders, and industry leaders will gather at Rebel Toronto for an evening that now spans two decades.

The 2026 Canadian Mortgage Awards (CMAs), presented by Canadian Mortgage Professional, will recognise outstanding work across 23 competitive categories, from broker specialists in private lending and reverse mortgages to the teams and technology companies reshaping the industry.

For the professionals shortlisted this year, the wait is almost over.

The night ahead

The evening begins at 6:00 p.m. with a cocktail reception on the first floor of Rebel Toronto, the waterfront event space at 11 Polson Street.

For an industry that spent much of 2025 navigating a historically concentrated wave of mortgage renewals, the reception offers something rarer: two hours to simply connect.

Guests are encouraged to arrive promptly, with the awards ceremony and dinner banquet commencing at 7:30 p.m.

The post-awards celebration runs from 10:30 p.m. onwards, giving the night room to breathe well past the final announcement.

The 2026 host is Sonia Mangat, a broadcaster and storyteller with a decade of experience across news, entertainment, and live event hosting in Canada.

Mangat currently appears on eTalk and CP24 Breakfast and has hosted high-profile stages including the Canadian Screen Awards.

As a skilled interviewer who has sat down with A-list celebrities, she brings the kind of relaxed authority a room of mortgage professionals tends to respond to – someone who commands attention without demanding deference.

Entertainment for the evening includes Soulfire, a five-piece live band specialising in classic rock, soul, Motown, disco, and Top 40 hits.

The dress code is formal: tuxedo, business suit, long gown, cocktail dress, or traditional attire. For those seeking a rental, the event has partnered with The Fitzroy Dress Rental, offering a 10 per cent discount with the code CMA26.

Secure a table at the 2026 Canadian Mortgage Awards and celebrate your team’s achievements alongside industry leaders, innovators, and top-performing professionals from across the country. #MortgageAwardsCA Book your table today: https://t.co/SSKx4yuft5 https://t.co/f31Lgyrrzt — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 28, 2026

Voices from past ceremonies

For Akshay Gupta, a commercial real estate mortgage agent at Foundry Mortgage Capital Corp. in Toronto and the 2025 Young Achiever of the Year, the CMA win carried practical weight beyond the gala night itself.

"Developers and investors need confidence in their advisor from day one," Gupta said.

"The CMA win signals that the work has been independently validated at a national level, which opens doors and shortens the trust-building process in a way that's otherwise difficult to manufacture."

Dalia Barsoum of Streetwise Mortgages, who took out both the Ontario and national Broker of the Year awards at the 2024 edition, pointed to what the recognition meant in a market that had just come through a difficult year.

"Especially as 2023 was a very challenging year in the industry, this award has a very special meaning right now," Barsoum said.

"Creative solutions for clients, really pushing through tough files, helping my team ride the wave and sticking together as a team were some things that I believe we did really well this year."

The spirit of community that runs through the awards was articulated at the 2024 gala by Carey Benvenuti of Lending Niagara – Mortgage Architects, who won the philanthropy category.

"The gift of giving is the gift that you give yourself," Benvenuti said.

Joe White, chief executive officer at the Real Estate and Mortgage Institute of Canada (REMIC) in Toronto, which sponsors the Broker of the Year award, captured the purpose of the evening plainly: "This award is the cream of the crop. It's something the industry needs to embrace and joyfully talk about – those helping Canadians with homeownership and financial freedom."

A milestone moment for the industry

The 2026 CMAs mark the programme's 20th anniversary – a milestone that coincides with one of the most structurally consequential periods in the Canadian mortgage market's recent history. 

Shawn Allen, founder of Matrix Mortgage Global and a past CMA sponsor, has spoken about the role these gatherings play after periods of industry stress.

"The industry went through a hard time with COVID, and now we need to show solidarity," Allen said.

"These awards are about giving back and celebrating achievements." That instinct – to mark what the industry has built and who has built it well – is what twenty years of Canadian Mortgage Awards have institutionalised.

The 2026 programme spans 26 categories in total, including the Haventree Bank Award for Lifetime Achievement, which carries no nominated finalists and is announced only on the night.

Sponsors backing the programme include CMI Canadian Mortgages Inc., Equitable Bank, Haventree Bank, MCAN Mortgage Corporation, RFA Mortgage Corporation, and Real Property Solutions Inc. (RPS).

Winners will be revealed live at Rebel Toronto on November 25 and published the same night across CMP's channels.

Registration for the November 25 gala is open at canadianmortgageawards.com.

items.description: EQB offloads its equipment leasing arm to Desjardins as it sharpens focus on core growth
items.content: <p>EQB offloads its equipment leasing arm to Desjardins as it sharpens focus on core growth</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639288916419378197.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: EQB offloads its equipment leasing arm to Desjardins as it sharpens focus on core growth
items.body:
Equitable Bank, the Toronto-based lender that routes its alternative mortgages exclusively through Canada’s broker channel, has agreed to sell its commercial equipment leasing subsidiary, Bennington Financial Corp., to Desjardins Group.

The deal marks another step in EQB Inc.’s deliberate exit from non-core businesses. It follows their acquisition of PC Financial, which closed in July and added nearly four million customers.

Desjardins Group will acquire 100% of Bennington’s shares at a price equivalent to an approximately 8% discount to lease receivables.

As at July 31, Bennington’s aggregate portfolio held roughly $1.1 billion in lease receivables. The transaction is expected to close in the first half of 2027. 

EQB will reclassify Bennington as held for sale and record a net after-tax charge in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, treated as an adjusting item.

The deal is expected to be relatively neutral to Equitable Bank’s common equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital ratio at closing.

Chadwick Westlake, President and Chief Executive Officer of EQB Inc. in Toronto, Ontario, said the divestiture is a natural extension of the bank’s recalibrated priorities.

“At EQB, we’re focused on doing more of what we do best and investing where we see the greatest opportunity to win,” he said.

“This transaction allows us to further concentrate our capital and resources on our core growth priorities, particularly following our PC Financial transaction. It also positions Bennington with an owner that is equipped to grow the business to its full potential with expertise in the sector. Consistent with other businesses and product exits over the past year, this move strengthens our ability to create value for customers and shareholders over the long term.”

A pattern of deliberate portfolio exits

The Bennington sale continues a visible pivot at EQB. Since completing the acquisition of PC Financial, EQB has moved steadily to shed businesses that no longer align with its core focus.

Canadian Mortgage Professional has followed EQB’s most profitable year on record, when annual revenue surpassed $1 billion for the first time in fiscal 2025.

The broker channel remains central to that model; as one Equitable Bank executive previously confirmed to Canadian Mortgage Professional, “We continue to believe that the best way in this country to get a mortgage is through a mortgage broker.”

A strategic fit for Desjardins

Denis Dubois, President and CEO of Desjardins Group in Lévis, Québec, said the deal complements the cooperative’s existing business financing capabilities.

“Bennington’s specialized expertise in commercial equipment leasing and financing makes it a strong strategic fit for Desjardins,” he said.

“This transaction brings capabilities that complement our existing business financing offering and support our growth ambitions across Canada, while providing a strong foundation for Bennington to continue building on its established business, expertise and relationships.”

Desjardins Group is a financial cooperative, offering personal and business banking, wealth management, and insurance services to more than 10 million members and clients, with total net revenue of $16.31 billion and total assets of $510.2 billion in fiscal 2025.

National Bank Capital Markets and McCarthy Tétrault LLP are advising EQB on the transaction. Desjardins Capital Markets and Norton Rose Fulbright Canada LLP are advising Desjardins.

items.title: Prime rate hits 4.70% today as big banks act on BoC hike
items.description: Variable-rate mortgage and HELOC borrowers face higher costs today as Canada’s big six banks move
items.content: <p>Variable-rate mortgage and HELOC borrowers face higher costs today as Canada’s big six banks move</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639288897773939059.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Variable-rate mortgage and HELOC borrowers face higher costs today as Canada’s big six banks move
items.body:
Canada’s variable-rate mortgage holders and home equity line of credit (HELOC) borrowers are paying more as of today, after the country’s six largest banks put a new prime lending rate of 4.70% into effect. 

The move follows the Bank of Canada’s (BoC) decision to raise its overnight rate by 25 basis points to 2.50% on Wednesday, its first increase since 2023.

The Royal Bank of Canada (RBC), Toronto-Dominion Bank (TD), Bank of Montreal (BMO), Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce (CIBC), Bank of Nova Scotia (Scotiabank), and National Bank of Canada each implemented the quarter-point increase, moving in lockstep from a prime rate of 4.45% that had been in place since October 2025.

TD also raised its separate mortgage prime rate — the benchmark used to price its variable-rate mortgage products — to 4.85% from 4.60%, a spread that sits 15 basis points above its standard prime.

For borrowers on fixed-payment variable mortgages, today’s change means a larger share of each instalment goes toward interest rather than principal. Those on adjustable-payment structures will see monthly costs rise immediately.

A housing market that wasn’t moving before today

The effective rate increase reaches a market that had already gone quiet.

Phil Soper, president and chief executive of Royal LePage in Toronto, told Canadian Mortgage Professional this month that anticipated buyer pull-ahead had not materialised even as rate-hike speculation intensified.

“You’d see some people that were planning to get into the market in the spring of 2027, for example, jumping in now to get ahead of anticipated higher borrowing costs. Yet we’re not seeing material changes in the trajectory of transaction volumes. It’s very flat,” Soper said.

Benjamin Reitzes of BMO says the Bank of Canada's first rate hike in more than three years may not be its last, with future decisions likely hinging on economic growth, inflation trends, and incoming data over the months ahead. https://t.co/lcW0HncB9d — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 29, 2026

What brokers need to tell clients today

Leah Zlatkin, mortgage broker and expert at LowestRates.ca, said in April that borrower psychology still carries heavy residue from the previous hiking cycle.

“Most borrowers still prefer the certainty of fixed payments, especially after the sharp increases to variable rates during the Bank of Canada’s rate-hiking cycle in 2022 and 2023,” Zlatkin said. That hesitancy only deepens with today’s move confirmed.

“Variable rates come with uncertainty,” she added. “Borrowers need to be comfortable with the possibility that rates could move higher again depending on how the economic environment evolves.”

Victor Tran, spokesperson at Rates.ca, shared earlier this year that despite growing curiosity around variable products, fixed-rate mortgages still dominate client decisions.

“Most households are still opting for fixed because it offers predictability in an environment where rate direction isn’t guaranteed,” Tran said.

items.title: How rising rates could impact Canada’s mortgage market outlook
items.description: What higher borrowing costs could mean for homebuying and the renewal wave
items.content: <p>What higher borrowing costs could mean for homebuying and the renewal wave</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639288862172865356.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: What higher borrowing costs could mean for homebuying and the renewal wave
items.body:
Fixed mortgage rates have been on the rise amid climbing bond yields in recent weeks and the Bank of Canada is now back in hiking mode, putting upward pressure on variable rates.

National homebuying activity was already weak before the central bank’s 25-basis-point hike on Wednesday, but mortgage industry figures fear the move could worsen the outlook for the housing market even further.

The Canadian Mortgage Brokers Association of Ontario (CMBA-ON) said it was “disappointed” by the BoC’s move, describing it as a decision that could have a big negative impact on consumer and investor confidence in a market that’s already been weighed down by global economic uncertainty and trade tensions.

Jessica Rickerby, CMBA-ON president, suggested that the decision had prioritized inflation over housing challenges. “While inflation is a key concern of Ontarians, so is housing affordability,” she said in remarks accompanying the statement.

“The difference is that affordability is a pressing issue right now, whereas inflation is – at present – only slightly above the Bank of Canada’s target rate.”

Higher rates have implications for the renewal picture

The recent jump in fixed rates has seen a growing number of Canadians turn away from those options and toward sometimes shorter-term variable options, a trend noted by Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) in its latest residential mortgage industry report.

The much-discussed mortgage renewal wave, in which scores of pandemic-era mortgages have renewed at higher interest rates in 2025 and 2026, seemed to be past its peak. But if rates continue rising – and Canadians are increasingly choosing shorter mortgage terms – that could prolong renewal challenges, according to CMHC’s deputy chief economist Aled ab Iorwerth (pictured top).

“There is a move away from the five-year fixed towards shorter-term mortgages,” he told Canadian Mortgage Professional. “And interest rates have been going up. So I’m a little bit more concerned than I used to be in that area.

“I’m a little bit concerned that we’re going to have more of this discussion of renewal at higher interest rates. Perhaps my concerns won’t materialize – and I hope they don’t – but that is certainly an area that I’m more concerned about than I used to be.”

That’s not to say a series of big rate hikes by the Bank of Canada is in store. Instead, ab Iorwerth’s main concern is wider pressure in the lending system with the potential to drive bond yields and interest rates higher.

“US fiscal deficits, demand for money for AI, saving from an aging population – I see a lot of demand for savings, putting upward pressure on, say, five-year interest rates,” he said. “I wouldn’t tie it directly to the Bank of Canada. There’s going to be a lot of demand for money in order to invest in a range of different options.”

Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, the BoC’s senior deputy governor Carolyn Rogers indicated the central bank wasn’t expecting the housing market to pick up pace any time soon.

“Certainly, borrowing rates are currently weighing a bit on the housing market,” Rogers said after the Bank’s announcement. “An increase will add to that a bit on the margin, so I think the outlook we’ve got for housing in the forecast… takes all of that into account.”

What the hike means for commercial mortgages

Rising bond yields and inflation concerns have clouded the outlook for the commercial lending sector – but Mark Fieder, principal and president at Avison Young Canada, struck a bullish tone on the space’s prospects after the BoC’s latest move.

“Despite this rate hike, we anticipate demand for institutional-quality commercial real estate will remain strong,” he said, “supported by durable income, downside protection, and long-term portfolio stability.

“Pricing for premier assets will stay competitive, particularly in the industrial and multifamily sectors. Transaction activity will be increasingly governed by asset quality, lease profile, and growth prospects.”

items.title: Award-Winning Flemingdon Park Office-Turned-Rental Makes A Case For Conversions
items.description:
Located in Toronto’s Flemingdon Park neighbourhood, e-lofts — a 15-storey office-to-residential conversion project — has won a coveted Ontario Home Builders’ Association (OHBA) award in its final months of construction.

The purpose-built rental development, which was first proposed in spring 2025, was awarded High-Rise Building of the Year at the OHBA’s 2026 Awards of Distinction Gala for “outstanding architecture, innovation, and design excellence,” according to a press release from the project’s developer, Amexon Developments. The win is significant given the low number of adaptive reuse projects in the province.

Office-to-residential conversion was an idea that picked up speed at the tail end of the pandemic, when a record-high number of office buildings were sitting vacant, and more housing was desperately needed. Why not turn those vacant offices into apartments or condos?

Turns out, it’s a bit more complex than that. In Toronto, older office buildings tend to have physical characteristics that don’t support residential layouts. For example, offices often have deep floorplates that restrict sunlight from reaching the centre of the building, or they have too few elevators or insufficient plumbing capacity — all costly deficiencies that make demolitions more attractive by comparison.

Meanwhile, red tape, like Toronto’s office replacement requirements, and a lack of municipal grants, such as Calgary’s Downtown Office Conversion Program — which offers up to $75 per square foot for qualifying adaptive re-use projects — limit the financial and logistical viability of such retrofits.

Amexon’s e-lofts, however, is one of the exceptions. “Not all buildings are suitable for conversion — this one is exceptional because it has all the right attributes to support a successful conversion into residential lofts,” says Ashling Evans, vice president of real estate at Amexon Developments. “With over 300,000 sq. ft of buildable area, infrastructure costs can be efficiently distributed across 331 units.” In comparison, smaller buildings in the 100,000–200,000 sq.-ft-range often lack the economies of scale to make conversion financially viable.

e-lofts exterior

e-lofts fitness centre

On top of sheer size, the former Flemingdon Park office building’s design made an optimal foundation for residential living. “A centrally-located elevator core allows for optimal unit planning,” says Evans. “In contrast, many office buildings have off-centre cores that limit layout flexibility and make residential conversion inefficient or impossible.”

Aside from the challenging removal of the large, heavy precast exterior walls to allow for larger residential windows, Amexon sees the building’s commercial past as an advantage.

“The adaptive reuse approach takes advantage of the building’s existing structure to deliver housing faster and more sustainably than ground-up construction,” says Evans. It has been a speedy project, with occupancy expected in summer 2027, just over two years after the initial building application was filed. “Also, the loft-style suites at e-lofts will feature 12-foot floor-to-ceiling windows, polished concrete floors, exposed spiral ductwork, and structural elements for an industrial-chic aesthetic,” she adds.

Another integral aspect of the retrofit is a whole host of eco-friendly updates, including carbon-free mechanical systems that improve air quality and efficiency, green roofs and rainwater harvesting systems, and EV charging stations installed at every parking space.

e-lofts coworking space

Also available to residents will be an array of amenities. This includes a fitness centre, co-working spaces, pet daycare, and a 12,000-sq.-ft. rooftop patio with a saltwater pool, lounge areas, communal herb garden, and outdoor fitness zones.

While office-to-residential conversions haven’t taken off the way it once seemed they would, e-lofts serves as a rare example that, when physical design and financial logistics align, commercial spaces can be given new life.
