items.title: The big question: How many more BoC rate hikes are ahead?
items.description: The central bank delivered a 25-basis-point increase on Wednesday, and it may not be done yet
items.content: <p>The central bank delivered a 25-basis-point increase on Wednesday, and it may not be done yet</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639288097708752714.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: The central bank delivered a 25-basis-point increase on Wednesday, and it may not be done yet
items.body:
The Bank of Canada delivered its first interest rate hike for over three years on Wednesday, sparking immediate questions about how far – and how fast – it might raise rates if it decides further increases are needed.

The central bank’s decision moved its benchmark rate to 2.5%, and its accompanying statement was frank that more hikes could be ahead if the inflation outlook worsens again.

For now, much will depend on the economic and inflation data that emerges in the months ahead, Bank of Montreal (BMO) managing director, Canadian rates and macro strategist Benjamin Reitzes told Canadian Mortgage Professional.

“It’s a little bit early to say how far they’ll go,” Reitzes said. “Looking at market pricing, there’s [a benchmark rate of] about 3.5% by the end of next year, a little further out. And that’s a bit on the aggressive side, I think.

“Getting that high suggests that you’d need a trade deal and some pretty good economic outcomes for that to come to fruition.”

At least one more hike seemingly ahead

It’s still safe to assume that the central bank will raise rates at least once more in the next several months, Reitzes said, either in December or January. The extent of the economy’s weakness in the coming weeks will be a crucial deciding factor in the timing of the next hike.

“The reason for their caution is that they have a pretty soft [GDP] forecast for the fourth quarter, just 0.8% growth,” he said. “If you have that amount of softness in the economy, do they really want to be hiking rates in that environment? The answer is probably no.

“They want to make sure that there is a rebound in growth. So if we do get some numbers coming over the next few weeks that point to a better fourth quarter, then that would be enough for them to likely [hike]. But we don’t get a lot of pieces of information between now and December, unfortunately.”

Central bank governor Tiff Macklem highlighted that persistent lack of clarity in remarks at the press conference following the announcement – a situation that’s exacerbated by ongoing geopolitical chaos.

“We are mindful that uncertainty is still elevated,” he said. “Developments in the Middle East and Canada-US trade relations both remain fluid.”

Inflation concerns persist amid rising fuel costs

The annual inflation rate ticked higher in September, increasing to 3.1% amid continuing upward pressure on fuel prices caused by the US-Iran war.

Some economists viewed that as a mild enough reading for the BoC to keep rates steady in today’s announcement, but a growing number indicated a pre-emptive increase by the central bank was the likeliest outcome of its October decision.

Macklem said fuel costs would probably start to impact other types of inflation if they remain elevated. “The longer energy prices remain high, the more likely it is these costs will spill over to consumer prices more broadly,” he said.

But the consumer price index (CPI) is still well below its 2022 level, when it ballooned to a 39-year high and prompted a flurry of big BoC rate hikes. The current environment, Reitzes said, is a “different world” to that era – mainly because of the weak growth outlook.

That means a steady stream of rate hikes by the central bank in the coming months remains unlikely for now.

“The likelihood of that resuming or something like that seems pretty low. We don’t have the level of stimulus globally that we had in the economy at that time,” he said. “You don’t have governments around the world pouring money into the economy and the post-pandemic surge in demand.

“We don’t have that type of event coming at this point. It’s more energy-price-driven. And we’ll see how the war in the Middle East goes. It’s just not the same backdrop – and the Bank just wants to make sure that they don’t let inflation take root again and have to deal with broader price pressures and then have to raise rates more aggressively later.”

items.title: BoC warns of 'subdued' outlook for housing market as rate hike raises borrowing costs
items.description: The Bank of Canada's rate hike Wednesday is set to translate to higher borrowing costs for homebuyers, adding further pressure as the real estate sector also copes with rising prices for construction materials.
items._ogDesc: The Bank of Canada's rate hike Wednesday is set to translate to higher borrowing costs for homebuyers, adding further pressure as the real estate sector also copes with rising prices for construction materials.
items.body:
The Bank of Canada's rate hike Wednesday is set to translate to higher borrowing costs for homebuyers, adding further pressure as the real estate sector also copes with rising prices for construction materials.

The central bank raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter-point to 2.5 per cent, the first increase in more than three years, as it warned that inflation driven by the war in the Middle East is likely to spread.

"There's a number of things weighing on housing right now," the bank's senior deputy governor Carolyn Rogers told reporters, as she described a "subdued" outlook for the sector.

"Certainly, borrowing rates are currently weighing a bit on the housing market. An increase will add to that a bit on the margin, so I think the outlook we've got for housing in the forecast here takes all of that into account."

The big question is whether the central bank's move is a one-time adjustment or the start of a sustained tightening cycle, said Phil Soper, president and CEO of real estate firm Royal LePage.

He said the sector's "prolonged weakness is already weighing on economic growth, and higher borrowing costs will only deepen that challenge."

Shawn Zigelstein, a broker for Royal LePage Signature Realty, said he believes the rate hike won't have a major effect on consumer confidence just yet.

"It's not like we are in a market like we were back in 2022 where the prices are increasing substantially on a regular basis," he said in an interview.

"A quarter-point adjustment really shouldn't make too much of a difference on someone's mortgage payments at this point."

The central bank's key policy rate had held steady for nearly a year following a series of cuts. Inflation ticked up to 3.1 per cent in September due to high gas prices, and the bank said an increase to the rate is necessary to reduce the risk that elevated energy prices spill over to other goods and services.

Zigelstein said clients he speaks with are more concerned about other day-to-day costs and whether the overall inflation environment makes it the right time to buy a home.

"They have been worried about other factors, including tariffs and such. Are they going to have the jobs that they had? Are their investments going to do what they've been doing? So they've got bigger concerns than worrying about interest rates," he said.

"Now, of course, if the rates start to change a little bit, then we will start to see potentially a little bit of a pullback on what people are spending because borrowing costs will be higher."

While Canada "is not facing a broad mortgage crisis," there are signs of financial pressure concentrated in specific regions such as the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area and southwestern Ontario, said Aled ab Iorwerth, deputy chief economist for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corp., earlier this week.

He said trade tensions are weighing on key manufacturing sectors such as the automotive industry in those areas, leading to labour-market uncertainty and softer housing market conditions.

CMHC said Ontario's mortgage arrears rate reached 0.32 per cent in the second quarter, which is still below historical peaks but expected to continue rising through mid-2027. British Columbia and Atlantic Canada are expected to see a more moderate rise in mortgage arrears over the same period.

"The mortgage system is adjusting, but these early warning signs, particularly in parts of Ontario, need to be monitored closely," ab Iorwerth said in a news release.

Don Kottick, president of Re/Max Canada, said that while an interest-rate increase "may give some buyers pause," more balanced market conditions in many regions are creating opportunities for buyers, including greater choice and room to negotiate.

In September, the national average sale price fell 1.6 per cent year-over-year to $666,538, according to the Canadian Real Estate Association. National home sales were down 7.7 per cent from the same month last year, as the association cited higher fixed mortgage rates and the Bank of Canada's "notably more hawkish tone."

Fixed rates are largely unaffected by the Bank of Canada's decision, having already moved higher in recent months in line with the bond market. But further movement in the bond market into 2027 could prompt mortgage costs to jump, which "would have a dampening impact on home purchases," said Michael Waters, CEO of Minto Group, a real estate developer.

"Higher rates, everything else held equal, will reduce levels of purchaser activity for anything durable of size — cars and houses, certainly," Waters said in an interview.

"The housing sector is very slow right now and so that obviously would be a concern for anyone in that sector."

Meanwhile, the central bank said Wednesday that higher energy and import costs are expected to raise the costs of housing construction and maintenance through higher prices for materials and equipment.

Any increase to the cost of credit will also have an effect on the ability to build new projects, particularly new housing and supporting infrastructure, said Nicole Emmett, vice-president of communications, marketing and member services for the Canadian Construction Association.

"A home isn’t a home without the roads, sewers and watermains that support it, and higher borrowing costs put pressure on the margins of the contractors building them, which are already stretched by global supply chain disruptions and material costs," she said in a statement.

"Many contractors also rely on financing for equipment, materials and day-to-day operations."

Waters said higher interest — construction loans are based on a floating rate — along with rising input costs "will squeeze margins" and potentially lead to fewer large-scale project completions in the coming years.

"Certainly projects are far more challenged today than they would have been six months ago, pre-Iran war," he said.

"The impact would be fewer projects meeting economic feasibility tests and more projects probably sitting idle until market conditions improve, so that could have a negative impact on the creation of new housing supply."

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 28, 2026.

Sammy Hudes, The Canadian Press

items.title: Canadian household credit defies renewal shock, CIBC finds
items.description: Mortgage arrears keep rising, but CIBC economists see few cracks across the wider household credit picture
items.content: <p>Mortgage arrears keep rising, but CIBC economists see few cracks across the wider household credit picture</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639288083080510285.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Mortgage arrears keep rising, but CIBC economists see few cracks across the wider household credit picture
items.body:
Canadian borrowers are absorbing the mortgage renewal shock better than most forecasters expected.

Credit scores are improving and early-stage delinquencies are easing, even as more homeowners fall seriously behind on their mortgages.

That is the conclusion of a new report from CIBC Capital Markets economists Benjamin Tal and Katherine Judge, who revisited household credit quality a year into the mortgage payment cliff.

Their verdict came two days before the Bank of Canada raised its overnight rate to 2.5%.

“Simply put, the credit quality position of Canadian households is surprising on the upside,” they wrote.

Mortgage arrears remain the weak spot

The exception is the mortgage book itself. The share of mortgages 90 or more days in arrears keeps climbing and now sits well above its pre-pandemic level, as borrowers renew at higher rates into a softer labour market.

CIBC estimates that payment jumps of more than 40% hit 5% to 6% of all outstanding mortgages in 2026.

Regionally, the strain is uneven, with mortgage arrears in Ontario expected to keep worsening until mid-2027.

“I think [delinquencies] will continue to increase as more homeowners renew their mortgages in the next 12 months, 24 months even. But I think it’s going to be a slow grind,” Victor Tran, mortgage and real estate expert at Rates.ca, told Canadian Mortgage Professional earlier this year.

Still, serious delinquencies on credit cards and lines of credit held by mortgage borrowers have levelled off. Because most households stop paying those debts before missing a mortgage payment, CIBC treats them as an early warning, and that warning has gone quieter.

Derek Serra of Westboro Mortgage Investment Corporation says the Canadian housing market is still feeling the effects of pandemic-era low interest rates, as borrowers face higher renewal costs and affordability challenges. https://t.co/Dcwt1JphsT — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 28, 2026

Proposals, not bankruptcies

Elsewhere, the numbers point to normalization rather than distress.

Household debt is growing at about 4%, near a record low outside the pandemic, and mortgage balances rose roughly 2% year over year in August, the weakest pace in 25 years. Average credit scores sit 1.3% above 2019 levels.

Insolvencies are up 6% over the year but are only now approaching 2019 levels.

Consumer proposals, which typically cost lenders less than bankruptcies, made up 77% of filings in the third quarter, compared with 60% in 2019. Equifax data on Canada’s insolvency hotspots suggests that choice is deliberate.

“A lot of the insolvency rates that we’re seeing an increase in is really tied to homeowners that want to protect their assets but obviously have a mountain of non-mortgage debt, and they’re trying to find a way to formally reduce that through more structured payments so that they can stay afloat,” Kathy Catsiliras, Equifax Canada’s vice-president of analytics and consulting, told CMP.

CIBC expects renewal payment increases to ease notably from February 2027, with mortgage delinquencies likely to trend lower that year, depending on the job market.

Until then, the Bank of Canada’s first rate hike since 2023 adds pressure where households are already stretched, according to Joel Fox, chief operating officer of Ownright.

“For most people, the 25 basis points on its own isn’t a dramatic change by any means. On a $500,000 mortgage, it’s roughly $60 to $70 more a month, depending on the amortization. The problem is that it can really affect households that have already been struggling,” Fox said.

“Plenty of people locked in at very low rates a few years ago, and they’re now renewing into a much bigger payment. This hike doesn’t help.”

His advice for borrowers nearing renewal: “If you’re renewing in the next year, start early. It’s a good idea to talk to your lender or broker, compare offers and know what your payment will be before the renewal notice shows up. Pick something you can live with instead of hoping and waiting for rates to fall.”

In partnership with Colliers as a Presenting Sponsor, STOREYS announces Top 75 Real Estate Projects, a new annual report and program built to recognize the most meaningful real estate projects across Canada – from landmark new-builds and redevelopments through to masterplans reshaping entire neighbourhoods, encompassing iconic office buildings, niche industrial centres, master-planned communities, and mixed-use assets.

STOREYS, now in its tenth year, is taking a format with more than two decades of history to the private sector. Top 75 Real Estate Projects builds on the Top 100 Infrastructure Projects report from sister publication ReNew Canada, a mainstay of public sector infrastructure coverage. Now, for the first time, that national framework, editorial rigour, and Top Projects format are being applied to the country’s most significant real estate developments.

items._ogDesc: The fintech secures fresh backing as its client base grows to 4 million Canadians
items.body:
Wealthsimple Technologies Inc. has closed an equity round of up to CAD $425 million at a post-money valuation of CAD $13.8 billion. That's nearly 40% above the CAD $10 billion mark the Toronto-based financial technology company reached in October 2025.

GIC, the Singapore sovereign wealth fund that co-led last year’s fundraise, is again leading the round, alongside Power Corporation of Canada, IGM Financial Inc., ICONIQ, Canada Pension Plan Investment Board (CPP Investments) and Inovia.

The deal is structured as a CAD $300 million primary offering alongside a secondary component of up to CAD $125 million, an arrangement designed to let employees share in the value they have helped create.

“This raise reflects the deep conviction our partners have in Wealthsimple’s mission and in our role as the company defining the future of financial services in Canada,” said Michael Katchen, CEO and co-founder of Wealthsimple, in Toronto.

“These investors know our business deeply and chose to increase their commitment. With their support, we will keep building and innovating until every Canadian can live their entire financial life on Wealthsimple.”

Leaving the banks behind

As of September 30, Wealthsimple held CAD $169.2 billion in assets under administration, up 69% from CAD $100 billion at the time of its October 2025 fundraise.

The company now serves more than 4 million Canadians, including one in four aged 18 to 40.

In Q2 2026, new chequing account openings outpaced new investment accounts for the first time in the company’s history.

What it means for mortgage brokers

Wealthsimple’s growing product suite includes a Portfolio Line of Credit, allowing clients to borrow against their investment holdings, alongside a business chequing account, a prepaid Visa card and cash deposit access at more than 5,300 Canada Post locations across Canada.

In the past year, the company launched more than 50 new products spanning trading, chequing and business tools.

As Canadian mortgage industry observers track how fintechs are gaining ground in the mortgage market, the concern is as much about where clients park their savings and equity as it is about which lender wins the deal.

That shift has been closely followed by the sector. Naga Parvatharajan, chief executive of Ratehub.ca in Toronto, told Canadian Mortgage Professional earlier this year – while discussing how OSFI’s new approvals framework is opening the market to fintechs – that greater competition among financial institutions means Canadians gain “better rates and innovative options,” a dynamic that has historically served the broker channel well.

Tanya Woods, head of government and regulatory affairs and policy counsel at Questrade Financial Group, in Toronto, offered broader context to CMP when examining what open banking could mean for Canada’s mortgage market in the years ahead.

" The fact that Canadians might be able to see their entire financial picture on a single dashboard one day is very exciting because they will have a much greater sense of what they can afford and where the opportunities in their financial picture [are], so that they can make different or better decisions on housing," she said.

"Maybe they can afford more than they realized. Maybe they can find new ways to structure their debt because they get a better picture of the types of debt load that they’re carrying and where they can reduce it or leverage it positively. There’s so much opportunity."

items.title: Canada’s rate hike deepens broker worry over a struggling housing market
items.description: Economists call the move preventative; mortgage brokers say affordability remains the real crisis
items.content: <p>Economists call the move preventative; mortgage brokers say affordability remains the real crisis</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639288054691670926.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Economists call the move preventative; mortgage brokers say affordability remains the real crisis
items.body:
The Bank of Canada raised its overnight rate by 25 basis points to 2.5% on October 28, 2026, its first increase since 2023, framing the decision as risk management against building inflationary pressure rather than the beginning of a sustained tightening cycle.

Governor Tiff Macklem was direct in his reasoning: “The main argument for an increase was that energy prices are higher, they are expected to remain higher, and cost pressures are building.”

The October Monetary Policy Report (MPR) revised headline inflation to 3.5% by year-end, with the Bank’s 2% target now not expected until mid-2028.

GDP growth projections were upgraded to 1% for 2026 and 2% for 2027, with the Bank’s estimated neutral overnight rate range placed at 2.25% to 3.25%.

Economists divided on the next move

Earlier in the year, Bay Street analysts were actively debating whether a 2026 Bank of Canada rate hike was likely as oil-driven inflation pressure built. That question has now been answered. What remains contested is what follows.

Frances Donald, chief economist at Royal Bank of Canada in Toronto, and assistant chief economist Nathan Janzen described the decision as “preventative medicine,” noting the Bank’s own MPR acknowledged labour market slack and core inflation near 2%.

“The risks of future inflation were judged to have increased more than downside economic growth risk,” they wrote.

Marc Ercolao, economist at TD Economics in Toronto, characterised the hike as insurance-buying.

“We think this hike buys the Bank a few months to assess whether higher energy and input costs are actually filtering through to consumer prices,” he wrote, forecasting one additional 25-basis-point hike in Q1-2027 that would bring the policy rate to 2.75%, roughly the midpoint of the neutral range.

The central bank said on Wednesday morning it was raising that trendsetting interest rate by 25 basis points to a level of 2.50%, ending its long wait-and-see approach on the rate question. https://t.co/zVa5MRcPZe — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 28, 2026

CIBC economist Andrew Grantham projected a hold in December before a further move in January.

“We don’t expect that core measures of inflation will accelerate as much as the Bank fears, which should become more obvious early in 2027 and allow the Bank of Canada to then hold interest rates at 2.75% throughout the remainder of next year,” he wrote, adding that two-year bond yields barely moved in the wake of the decision.

Dr. Sherry Cooper, chief economist at Dominion Lending Centres in Vancouver, said the Bank was drawing a direct line to its own recent failures.

“The communications make it clear that the central bank wants to stay ahead of the curve and ‘avoid the debacle’ of 2022-23, when it was too late to raise the policy rate,” she wrote.

Bruno Valko, vice-president of national sales at RMG Mortgage Corporation in Toronto, questioned the Bank’s 2027 inflation projection of 3%, given that WTI crude had surged from approximately $67 per barrel in late February to over $100 per barrel following the US-Iran conflict.

With year-over-year comparisons in 2027 measured against an already elevated 2026 base, Valko argued the maths did not hold.

“Come 2027, when comparing oil prices to 2026, assuming oil continues to hover around $100 per barrel, I dispute the rationale around how inflation can average 3% when it’s currently 3.1%,” he wrote.

Brokers warn of market consequences

For the broker community managing Canada’s mounting 2026 mortgage renewal pressures, the hike arrives at a precarious moment.

Joel Fox, chief operating officer of Ownright, a Toronto-based digital real estate law platform, warned the decision deepens an already prolonged housing downturn.

“A rate hike likely locks us into year-over-year declines in housing activity for the rest of this year and into next, and I don’t see things turning until there’s a rate drop,” Fox said.

His advice to clients approaching renewal was clear, and with the December decision drawing closer, what the BoC’s next decision means for the mortgage market will be watched closely by brokers across the country.

“If you’re renewing in the next year, start early. It’s a good idea to talk to your lender or broker, compare offers and know what your payment will be before the renewal notice shows up,” Fox said.

The Canadian Mortgage Brokers Association of Ontario (CMBA Ontario) formally opposed the decision. President Jessica Rickerby said affordability was the crisis in hand, not a theoretical future one.

“While inflation is a key concern of Ontarians, so is housing affordability. The difference is that affordability is a pressing issue right now, whereas inflation is – at present – a hypothetical,” Rickerby said.

CMBA Ontario cited approximately 5,300 new home sales in the Greater Toronto Area in 2025, a record low and an 81% fall from normal levels, according to the association.

items._ogDesc: The Bank of Canada raised rates to 2.5%, forecasting elevated inflation into 2028 as higher costs keep housing activity weak and push shelter inflation higher.
items.body:
Canada’s central bank raised its key policy rate as it tries to tame rising inflation. The Bank of Canada (BoC) hiked its overnight rate 25 basis points to 2.5% this morning, its first hike in over 3 years. In the accompanying report, the BoC warns of elevated inflation into mid-2028. Higher input and financing costs will also keep housing activity weak while boosting shelter inflation.

Canadian Inflation Isn’t Expected To Return To Target Until 2028

The BoC sees elevated inflation into 2028. The latest forecast from the central bank shows CPI inflation above 3% through Q3 2027. That’s roughly a point higher than they anticipated in their July report. It isn’t expected to return to their 2% target rate until mid-2028. While elevated inflation has largely been confined to energy and related categories, the Bank expects those pressures to spread over the next year.

High energy prices are spreading into production, transportation, and imports. Businesses have absorbed much of the increase so far, but expect to pass more on to consumers over the next 12 months, warns the BoC. Even after energy inflation turns negative in late 2027, earlier cost increases will continue to work their way through supply chains and boost prices.

Source: Bank of Canada.

Canadian Housing Investment Forecast To Lag The Economy

Higher rates are seen putting a drag on one of the country’s biggest components of GDP—housing investment. Residential investment primarily consists of spending on new home construction and substantial renovation. This sector is seen averaging less than 1% growth in 2027 and 2028. In contrast, GDP growth is expected to be roughly 2% for both years. The whole economy isn’t expected to slow, but housing will underperform.

Weak demand and high input costs are the reasons they cite. A lack of affordability, slow population growth, and rising borrowing costs are seen hitting the brakes on the demand side. Meanwhile, higher energy costs and imported input costs will make construction more expensive, throttling building activity.

Weak Housing Activity Isn’t Expected To Slow Rising Shelter Costs

Weak housing investment isn’t expected to slow shelter service inflation. It’s forecast to rise from just over 1% at the end of 2026 to 2% in 2027, and remain near that level into 2028. Higher material, equipment, construction, and maintenance costs are seen as the primary driver. Rising borrowing costs are expected to add further upward pressure. Rent inflation is seen as one of the few moderating factors for shelter, but it only partially offsets the other factors.

The impact on home prices isn’t clear, but higher expenses and weak demand aren’t bullish. At the same time, weak activity doesn’t automatically lead to affordability improvements.

The BoC report leaves an inflationary issue untouched: how government-backed construction spending supports higher input costs. Large projects compete for workers, resources, equipment, and land—even as private housing demand weakens. That spending can limit the disinflationary relief normally associated with a slowdown, leaving input costs elevated despite weak qualified demand.

items.title: Here's what Tiff Macklem said after the BoC's rate hike
items.description: Macklem warns oil price shock and Middle East conflict demand a policy response
items.content: <p>Macklem warns oil price shock and Middle East conflict demand a policy response</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639288017115537128.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Macklem warns oil price shock and Middle East conflict demand a policy response
items.body:
The Bank of Canada raised its policy interest rate by 25 basis points to 2.5% on October 28, its first increase since July 2023, as Governor Tiff Macklem declared the central bank's commitment to price stability in "this period of global upheaval," anchoring the decision in a Middle East oil shock and unsettled Canada-US trade relations.

Speaking alongside Senior Deputy Governor Carolyn Rogers in Ottawa, Macklem identified two developments that had shifted the Bank's calculus since July 2026: a deteriorating inflation outlook, with oil prices expected to "remain higher for longer" as the Middle East conflict persisted, and a stronger domestic recovery despite US tariff pressure.

"We are mindful that uncertainty is still elevated," he said.

"Developments in the Middle East and Canada-US trade relations both remain fluid."

Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation has held near 3% since April and is projected to reach roughly 3.5% by year-end, with the 2% target not expected until mid-2028.

CPI excluding gasoline remains at 2.2% and core inflation sits near 2%.

"The longer energy prices remain high, the more likely it is these costs will spill over to consumer prices more broadly," Macklem said.

Oil, trade tensions, and the inflation risk that tipped the Bank's hand

Governing Council weighed that risk against solid economic data. Gross domestic product (GDP) grew 3.3% in the second quarter, with preliminary indicators pointing to about 2% growth in the third quarter, per the Bank of Canada's October 2026 Monetary Policy Report.

The unemployment rate has held near 6.5%, and full-year 2026 GDP growth is forecast at just 1% as US tariffs weigh on activity.

Not all forecasters agreed the moment called for action.Stéfane Marion, chief economist at National Bank of Canada (NBC) in Montréal, told the Mortgage Professionals Canada (MPC) conference in Calgary last week that core data argued for patience.

"Core inflation is still at 2%," he said.

"I don't think that the Bank of Canada should be hiking [on October 28] and if they do hike, they can't be too aggressive."

What the hike means for mortgage brokers

For Canadian mortgage brokers, the decision reshapes client conversations immediately.

Variable-rate mortgage holders will see payments rise as lenders' prime rates move from 4.45% to 4.70%, a shift that renewal discussions and rate-path strategy had been building toward all year, and Wednesday's announcement intensifies the pressure.

Leah Zlatkin, a Toronto-based licensed mortgage broker and expert commentator with LowestRates.ca, said one move is unlikely to be the last.

"If there is a hike, I do think it's going to be a cycle," Zlatkin said.

TD Bank economist Marc Ercolao, speaking from Toronto, said Macklem had telegraphed the outcome weeks earlier.

"It was Bank of Canada Governor Macklem's remarks a couple of weeks ago that likely tipped the scales towards today's decision to hike," Ercolao said.

"The Bank of Canada said it does not see a clear offramp to the conflict in the Middle East and is increasingly worried about the risks to inflation."

Governing Council signalled caution on what comes next, stopping short of any firm commitment to further action.

"Looking ahead, Governing Council agreed we would take future decisions one meeting at a time," Macklem said.

"There could be a need to raise the policy rate further, but given the uncertainties, we will proceed carefully."

The Bank's next rate decision is set on December 9.

items.title: Only 18% Of Young Canadians Fully Confident About Homebuying Finances: Survey
items.description:
Just 18% of Canadians aged 18 to 34 say they feel confident navigating all financial aspects of buying a home, according to the 2026 Zown Homeownership & Financial Confidence Survey, released Wednesday.

That compares with 35% of those aged 35 to 54 and 50% of those 55 and older.

Zown, an AI-powered real estate brokerage, conducted the survey from October 14 to 16 among 1,500 online adult Canadians who are members of the Angus Reid Forum.

The survey also found 40% of Canadians tapped into their long-term savings over the past year to cover expenses or unexpected costs.

Among those who did, 29% used the money for emergencies or unexpected expenses, and 22% for groceries and everyday purchases. Another 13% put it toward regular housing costs, including rent or mortgage payments.

Alberta had the highest share of respondents drawing on long-term savings, at 48%. Saskatchewan and Manitoba combined came in at 44%, followed by Ontario and British Columbia at 41% each, Atlantic Canada at 35%, and Quebec at 34%.

“Housing affordability isn’t just about the price of a home. It’s also about whether Canadians can afford to become homeowners in the first place,” said Rishard Rameez, founder and CEO of Zown.

“There’s a disconnect between the dream of homeownership and the financial reality many Canadians face. We’re asking people to save tens of thousands of dollars for a down payment when they’re already drawing on their savings to cover everyday expenses. That’s a fundamental challenge we can’t afford to overlook.”

For the younger group, saving and planning for a downpayment and understanding the ongoing costs after buying a home were the areas of least confidence, at 19% each. Knowing how much home they can afford came next at 18%, then knowing which homebuying incentives or programs they qualify for (14%) and understanding closing costs (10%).

Ownership makes a similar difference. Only 13% of Canadians who have never owned a home, but haven’t ruled it out, feel confident across every financial aspect of buying one, compared with 46% of current homeowners.

For those prospective buyers, the downpayment is the area of least confidence, cited by 30%. Understanding how much home they can afford follows at 18%, and the ongoing costs of homeownership at 14%.

Inflation is running higher and longer than the Bank projected in July. CPI inflation has hovered around 3% since April, and the Bank expects it to climb to about 3.5% by the end of the year, largely because of persistently high oil prices.

The conflict in the Middle East is now in its eighth month with no clear path to resolution. The Bank expects CPI inflation to average 3% in 2027, a full percentage point above its July projection, before easing to 2% in the middle of 2028.

Governing Council said the hike is meant to reduce the risk that high energy prices spread into the prices of other goods and services. It said further increases may be needed, but that it would proceed carefully given the uncertainty.

The economy has outperformed expectations. GDP grew 3.3% in the second quarter, and recent indicators point to about 2% growth in the third, both stronger than the Bank anticipated. Consumer spending held up despite slow population growth, and business investment rebounded on oil and gas activity and machinery and equipment spending. Unemployment has held around 6.5% for several months.

New US tariffs are expected to slow growth in the fourth quarter. The Bank projects the economy will grow 1% in 2026 and 2% in both 2027 and 2028, a somewhat stronger outlook than July’s, though Canada-US trade relations remain a major source of uncertainty.

Business investment, exports and fiscal measures are expected to drive the 2027 rebound. Housing, however, isn’t on that list. The Bank expects it to remain relatively weak, with consumption growth moderating as well.

items.title: Municipalities await future of housing law after change in B.C. government
items.description: The B.C. Conservatives have promised to return authority to local governments to determine where housing density will go.
items._ogDesc: The B.C. Conservatives have promised to return authority to local governments to determine where housing density will go.
items.body:
Local councils returning to work in the wake of the municipal election are waiting to see what a new B.C. Conservative government does with provincial housing legislation that forced them to redo their bylaws and official community plans.

During the campaign, the party promised to return authority to local governments to determine where housing density will go.

The promise was a step back from its threat a couple of years ago to repeal Bill 44, which was enacted by the NDP government in 2023 to stimulate housing starts.

The legislation required municipalities to amend their bylaws by mid 2024 to allow four to six units on single-family and duplex lots, effectively up-zoning most of the province.

It also outlawed public hearings for development projects that conform to official community plans.

The latter raised the ire of many residents, who felt they no longer had any say on what was being built around them.

Victoria Mayor Marianne Alto, who was re-elected for a second term, said the city is waiting to see if the next government has “profoundly different directives.”

She said the 2023 provincial changes fit well with the city’s existing approach to housing development.

“Frankly our own agendas were more assertive than that anyway,” she said, adding they also didn’t have any problem with the province setting housing targets.

“We knew we’d exceed them, which we have.”

The most recent data available shows the City of Victoria had issued 2,359 occupancy permits for new homes by late fall 2025, well ahead of the goal of 1,425. Victoria’s target is to issue 4,902 occupancy permits by 2028.

Alto said the city will continue on its current path, including policies geared at producing more affordable housing, until told otherwise.

She noted that the incoming provincial government has suggested it intends to push for more affordable housing. “I suspect that they’re probably going to look at ways to do that,” she said.

Across the border in Saanich, the Bill 44 changes and loss of public hearings were a big issue for many residents.

Outgoing Saanich Mayor Dean Murdock said revising the official community plan and zoning rules to accommodate what is called small-scale multi-unit housing — like townhouses and multi-plexes — was a lot of work for district staff.

Undoing it would also require a “significant” amount of work if that’s the direction the new provincial government chooses to go, he said.

The district also created policies to guide the application process around small-scale multi-unit housing, updating its building permit language. “Those things would all have to be revised,” he said.

“This could be a major diversion in terms of priorities that a future council may set.”

Murdock said new governments are typically “allergic to the policies of their predecessors,” so while they may recognize the value in creating more family-suitable housing, they’re likely to just rip apart the current legislation.

“The issues around housing availability and affordability are not going away, and they will be very much a pressure on a Conservative government, just as it has been for an NDP government,” he said.

The Conservatives have said they will remove red tape around housing construction, review the costs that slow it down, shorten approval times and overhaul the B.C. Energy Step Code, which sets energy-efficiency requirements for new buildings.

Mike Drummond, chief executive of the Urban Development Institute, the voice of the development industry, said blanket up-zoning had unintended consequences, such as making land assembly more difficult. “In the end, we believe municipalities should have more flexibility on where added density goes.”

Drummond is also keen to see the new government tackle some of the problems stalling projects, including building code changes and permanently removing the expansion of the PST to professional services such as architectural and engineering work. The proposed expansion, which was supposed to come into effect Oct. 1, was paused by the previous NDP government

Casey Edge, executive director of the Victoria Residential Builders Association, said he would like the provincial government to limit the cost charges that municipalities can set for developers. Such charges, which are collected for water, sanitary sewers, drainage, parks and transportation upgrades to service new development, add thousands to the cost of a home, Edge said.

Last term, Victoria council considered more than doubling the fees developers pay toward infrastructure needed to support new housing, including roads, water and sewer systems, drainage and parks.

Edge said the government should also look at replacing the Step Code, enforcing interpretation of its own building code and holding municipalities accountable for permit delays.

“There should be reasonable timelines for permits,” he said. “There is no reason a permit for a new single-family home takes two weeks in one municipality and months in another municipality.”

items._ogDesc: Canadian real estate prices fell in 8 of 9 provinces last month. Ontario and BC lead the 22.5% drop from peak, but the broader market is now sliding.
items.body:
Canada’s real estate correction has largely been concentrated in one province, but that may change soon. Canadian Real Estate Association (CREA) data shows prices fell in September. All but one province moved lower, with BC going from resilient to leading the way lower in the past year. Other provinces, some of which hit record highs in 2026, are now making sharp moves lower. An anomaly or is the rest of the market ready to correct too?

Canadian Real Estate Prices Have Dropped $189k Since Peak

Before the provincial breakdown, let’s quickly review the national data. Canadian home prices fell 0.9% (-$5,700) to $651,400 in September, 3.4% (-$22,700) lower than last year and a whopping 22.5% (-$189,000) below peak. As previously noted, the lion’s share of that downward pressure is in Ontario—and to a lesser extent, BC. However, other provinces may be ready to join the correction.

Only One Province Saw Prices Climb, Nova Scotia Abruptly Plunges

Canadian real estate prices: Monthly change in dollars, September 2026.

Source: CREA; Better Dwelling.

Home prices only climbed in 1 of CREA’s 9 provincial indexes. The PEI benchmark rose 1.4% (+$5.1k), but that follows a 4.0% (-$15.6k) drop in August. Bucking the trend and rolling back part of the largest drop in PEI’s history are two very different stories.

The remaining 8 of 9 CREA indexes showed declines. The largest monthly decline was in Nova Scotia (-2.7%; -$11.8k), driven by an abrupt plunge in Halifax. A 1.3% (-$4.9k) drop in Saskatchewan and Ontario’s 1.0% (-$7.6k), round out the three biggest drops lower last month.

Despite the broad declines, most provinces remain higher than last year. These gains are mostly concentrated in Eastern Canada, while the Prairies were stable. Newfoundland’s 5.5% (+$18.6k) climb puts it in the lead for annual growth. It was followed by Saskatchewan, which came in 2.8% (+$10.4k) higher than last year, and New Brunswick at 2.7% (+$9.1k).

Leading the way lower over the past year is BC, where September came in 4.7% (-$42.4k) lower than last year. Ontario followed with a 3.9% (-$29.6k) drop over the same period, followed by Nova Scotia, whose monthly plunge pushed prices 2.5% (-$11.0k) lower.

Canada’s Real Estate Correction Has Only Hit 2 Provinces So Far

Decline in home prices from peak, by province.

Source: CREA; Better Dwelling.

Not one province remains at peak, though Newfoundland is only 1.0% (-$3.7k) below its July 2026 record high. Despite peaking in the same month, PEI has plunged more than double at 2.7% (-$10.5k). Neither province is that far from the peak, and all but two provinces remain close to the record highs.

Ontario is one of those two, plunging 26.7% (-$268.8k) since its March 2022 peak. BC is a distant second, down 16.7% (-$174.3k). That massive 10-point gap highlights just how concentrated this “crash” actually is. Nova Scotia sits in third at just 4.1% (-$18.2k) below its peak. But remember, BC’s decline was in the single-digits until well into last year. Nova Scotia’s abrupt monthly plunge could mean a broader correction is just getting started.

Whether Canada’s housing slump has another leg lower is anyone’s guess. The national index is down 22.5% from peak, but only Ontario has seen a drop larger than that. It’s being called a historic, 4-year market correction—yet most provinces are still hugging their record highs. Ultimately, corrections occur to resolve market inefficiencies for buyers, not just a national model. Until regional markets make sense to local buyers, activity will remain tame.

items.title: Millennium Ups Proposed Kitsilano Rental Tower To 26 Storeys, Adding Hotel
items.description:
Vancouver-based Millennium Development has submitted a new rezoning application for their project in the Kitsilano neighbourhood of Vancouver, according to a rezoning application published by the City of Vancouver last week.

The subject site of the project is 2158-2170 W 1st Avenue, two parcels that form an internal site between Yew Street and Arbutus Street on the southern side of W 1st Avenue, a few blocks south of Kitsilano Beach.

BC Assessment records show that 2158 W 1st Avenue transacted in January 2024 for $6,000,000, while 2170 W 1st Avenue transacted in August 2024 for $22,500,000. Each parcel is occupied by an old rental building, and BC Assessment values the parcels at $2,574,000 and $11,190,000 respectively, for a total assessed value of $13,764,000 — half of the 2024 sale price.

In 2024, Millennium Development — the developer behind Olympic Village — submitted a rezoning application for a 20-storey rental tower with 185 units and 20% of the floor area provided as below-market rental. The rezoning was approved in June 2025, but the project did not advance, and Millennium — through Millennium Kitsilano Nominee Ltd. — has now submitted a new rezoning application.

2158-2170 W 1st Avenue in Vancouver. (Chris Dikeakos Architects, Millennium Development)

The site was previously rezoned from RM-4 (Residential) to CD-1 (Comprehensive Development) as part of the previous rezoning application — enacted on June 2, 2026 — and Millennium is now seeking to amend the existing CD-1 zoning to allow for a 26-storey mixed-use rental and hotel tower with a maximum height of 301 feet and a density of 8.73 FSR — up from the previous 212 ft and 6.8 FSR.

The rental component will include 121 units with a suite mix of 33 studio units, 41 one-bedroom units, 31 two-bedroom units, and 16 three-bedroom units. Of the 121 units, 97 will be market rental and 24 will be below-market rental. The units have average sizes of 415 sq. ft, 512 sq. ft, 777 sq. ft, and 1,096 sq. ft for the market rental units, while the average sizes for the below-market units are all larger.

The market rental component will be at the top of the tower and above the hotel component, which will have 99 suites from Levels 6 to 16 — 9 suites per floor. A hotel operator/brand has not been identified.

Below the hotel component will then be amenity space, followed by some additional market rental units and all of the below-market units. The ground floor of the building will include the lobby, plus 6,294 sq. ft of retail space.

Millennium says in the rezoning application that “The project does not trade housing for hotel space” and that it "delivers secured market and below-market rental housing while simultaneously addressing the City's documented hotel shortage." From the proposal, 64 rental units have been cut, and the hotel component is being added along with six additional storeys.

The site falls within the Kitsilano North - Area B sub-area of the Broadway Plan, which allows for a maximum height of 20 storeys, but Millennium cited the Vancouver Official Development Plan (ODP) — approved earlier this year — and the Residential High-Rise 1 land use designation, which allows for up to 26 storeys.

“This application is being considered under the Broadway Plan,” said the City of Vancouver in a note published alongside the rezoning application. “The application requests consideration of height and density beyond existing policy provisions and proposes a hotel use that is not contemplated under current policy.”

The rezoning application notes that “The amenity program has been expanded beyond typical residential standards (greater than 10%) to provide a broader range of spaces that support wellness, recreation, social interaction, and flexible day-to-day use for all residents,” saying that “This modest increase enhances livability without increasing residential density.”

Renderings of the proposal for 2158-2170 W 1st Avenue in Vancouver. (Chris Dikeakos Architects, Millennium Development)

Another notable change in the proposal is the addition of a third elevator, which Millennium says “ensures that daily vertical circulation meets service reliability and accessibility standards in a mixed-use building of this scale.” To accommodate the change, the tower floorplate has been increased from 6,800 sq. ft to 6,923 sq. ft.

“The proposed 6,923 sq. ft. tower floorplate is a deliberate design response that supports the long-term functionality and performance of the building,” the application notes. “The modest increase in floorplate size accommodates a third elevator, significantly improving operational resilience, reducing resident wait times, enhancing vertical transportation, enabling more efficient structural grids, improving unit layouts, and creating a cleaner architectural expression.”

Although there are now no longer minimum parking requirements, the developer is proposing to include 164 vehicle parking spaces and 339 bicycle parking spaces in a five-level underground parkade.

After publishing the rezoning application last week, the City of Vancouver is holding the Q&A period for the proposal from Wednesday, November 18 to Tuesday, December 1.

items.title: Costly Construction, Decades Of Delays: Canada’s Project Leaders Get A New Playbook
items.description:
For much of the past two decades, Canada approached major projects with a simple idea: write the contract well enough, and the project would essentially look after itself. Each risk sat with a party ready to handle it, so when something went wrong, everyone knew who to turn to.

But it hasn’t worked out that way. Canada is one of the most expensive places in the world to build, and paying top dollar still doesn’t keep projects from running late (and over budget). That’s a problem at any time, but an even bigger one today, with the transportation, water, energy, natural resource, military and information technology projects currently being planned carrying multi-billion-dollar price tags — not to mention stakes in trade, sovereignty, national unity, and climate change. For developers and city-builders, these are the projects that determine where and how growth happens.

“What we’ve learned, in the last five to 10 years in particular, is that the contract is not going to save everything,” says Matti Siemiatycki, Professor of Geography and Planning, and Director of the University of Toronto’s Infrastructure Institute at the School of Cities. “We’ve realized that contracting is really a relational business, and that the relational skills amongst the parties who are delivering the projects are central to their success.”

The reliance on contracts has roots. In the early 2000s, public-private partnerships, or P3s, became the default for major projects, and by Siemiatycki’s account, most jurisdictions set up dedicated P3 agencies (many required the model outright). He assures that P3s do have their place. They just don’t suit every project, but the industry tried to apply them to nearly everything.

This history leaves many of today’s senior project leaders in a challenging position. They came up during the P3 era with “excellent project management skills,” Siemiatycki says, “but they were trained in a world that was very adversarial.”

The Canadian Infrastructure Leadership Academy was built to help those leaders move from contract-first thinking to the relationship-driven work major projects now demand. Launched by U of T’s Infrastructure Institute at the School of Cities and the Rotman School of Management, it’s the only executive program built specifically for major project leaders in Canada. It’s designed for public and private sector leaders with 10 to 15 years of experience who are preparing to take on the largest projects in their organizations.

These industry players already know how to run a project, so the curriculum builds on that experience, with a heavy focus on leading one: building teams when several organizations share a project, understanding infrastructure as a system, rather than a linear Gantt chart, and recognizing the biases that lead projects to underestimate costs and overestimate benefits. Negotiation and conflict resolution get dedicated focus as well, “because so many of these projects end up in some form of litigation or conflict,” Siemiatycki says. Rotman’s Geoffrey Leonardelli, Professor of Organizational Behavior and Human Resource Management, brings the school’s executive leadership expertise to the faculty.

Over six months, the hybrid program combines three three-day in-person modules at Rotman in Toronto with monthly live online sessions, mentorship, a capstone project, and the chance to work through a real issue from participants’ own professional contexts.

Graduates earn a certificate from the Rotman School of Management.

Applications are open now for the inaugural cohort, which launches April 13, 2027. Siemiatycki and his team are reviewing applications as they come in, with the goal of building an intentionally diverse cohort of leaders from civil infrastructure, energy, natural resources, and industrial projects.

The program’s model has a track record abroad; the United Kingdom and Australia both run similar academies. The Canadian version is distinct, though, in that it’s shaped to suit how projects actually get built here. “If you don’t understand our culture and you don’t understand how we collaborate, the projects ultimately end up in miscommunication, and things going wrong,” Siemiatycki says. “Having the program be by Canadians, for Canadians is really important.”

When that collaboration breaks down, the companies at the table feel it. “The risk is borne by the company, especially for construction,” Siemiatycki explains. “And if it goes badly, they’re going to wear it.”

Further, the academy puts public and private sector leaders in the same room on purpose. Over six months, each side learns how the other thinks about a project, and both leave with a network to call on, if and when something goes sideways.

“Ultimately we’ll build a cohort of people that can deliver for Canada,” Siemiatycki says.

The first cohort is where that network begins. Looking forward, the plan is to grow the academy into a national program delivered locally across the country, with each new cohort adding leaders who know how to work across the public and private sides of a project. Many of the organizations Siemiatycki has spoken with already see their participation as an investment in the sector, as well as in their own teams.

As that network grows, more of the country’s major projects can be led by people who already understand how their counterparts think, and who know who to call when things get difficult. It’s the relational side of delivery Siemiatycki says the contract was never going to cover on its own.

Applications for the inaugural cohort are open now, and organizations ready to add their people to that network can nominate a member of their team to apply. Applications submitted by November 30 receive 20% off tuition.

items.title: Sutton Group Announces Strategic Partnership With Ace Project Marketing
items.description:
Led by entrepreneur Ross McCredie, Vancouver-based Sutton Group has announced that they are partnering with Kelowna-based Ace Project Marketing, the latest move by the McCredie-led real estate company as it continues to expand its horizons.

The partnership will see Ace’s project marketing expertise and experience working with developers join forces with Sutton’s national network of over 6,000 agents in a way that the two say will benefit developers, real estate agents, and homebuyers.

As part of the partnership, Ace Project Marketing will be launching Ace Everywhere, a project marketing program designed exclusively for Sutton Group’s agents.

The firms said in a press release that the "program combines Ace’s centralized strategy, marketing and production capabilities with local agents’ market knowledge, relationships and licensed sales expertise.”

The result is Sutton agents will have support to work with presales, and Ace will bring its expertise to new markets across the country.

“For developers, the partnership brings together Ace’s insights into purchaser expectations and its sales and marketing expertise with Sutton’s national reach,” the companies said. “This collaboration offers a trusted sales and marketing pipeline, helping developers connect their projects with prospective buyers and the agents who advise them. By streamlining projects and maximizing presale success rates, the partnership supports market-driven developments and long-term success.”

“Combining Sutton’s national network of 6,000 agents with Ace’s customized market intelligence and project marketing expertise allows us to deliver data-driven solutions grounded in a people-first approach,” said Ace CEO Chad MacTavish. “Ace Everywhere gives us a practical way to grow alongside Sutton’s agents, combining the strength of a national platform with the local expertise every development needs. It reflects our confidence in the long-term opportunity for Canadian housing and our commitment to building the capabilities to support it.”

Sutton Group CEO Ross McCredie (left) and Ace Project Marketing CEO Chad MacTavish (right).

The Sutton Group team and Ace Project Marketing team.

“This partnership with Ace combines Sutton’s deep local roots across Canada with expertise in new housing, exactly when it’s needed most,” added Sutton Group President James Innis. “With new-home construction starts and preconstruction sales facing significant headwinds, we’re helping shape much-needed housing solutions that reflect the needs of each community, and giving our agents new ways to support buyers through a changing market.”

Sutton Group

Commenting on the partnership, Sutton Group CEO Ross McCredie called it “an exciting step forward in enhancing the services within Canadian real estate” and part of the company’s “technology-driven approach” towards delivering unparalleled value and homeowner-focused solutions for Canadians.

Sutton Group has taken several steps forward in recent years, after McCredie — through McCredie Investments — acquired the company in 2023. McCredie has spent the past few years positioning the company for long-term success in a technology-driven world and pushing the company towards a wealth-management model.

Those moves include the November 2025 acquisition of Ottawa-based real estate data technology company Homicity. With the acquisition, Homicity Co-Founder and CEO Jamie Blades joined Sutton Group as VP of Technology & Partner Success.

This spring, the company then announced a partnership with American luxury real estate brokerage Elliman (formerly known as Douglas Elliman) that would see the two companies create a new two-way referral program for their agents.

That same month, Sutton Group also announced that myAbode — an AI-driven deal processing “operating system” for residential brokerages — was making a strategic investment in Sutton Group and providing its brokerage optimization technology to Sutton’s agents.

Sutton Group has also continued to expand its footprint, opening new offices in Surrey, West Vancouver, Kelowna, Calgary, Stratford, and Gatineau-Ottawa over the past 12 months.

items.title: Bank of Canada Study Warns Rate Cuts Mostly Create Demand, Not Supply
items.description:

The post Bank of Canada Study Warns Rate Cuts Mostly Create Demand, Not Supply appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: A Bank of Canada staff paper finds about 80% of the building boost from rate cuts comes from excess demand, and ignoring shelter inflation fuels booms.
items.body:
Canada’s real estate industry often argues the central bank should ignore shelter inflation and keep rates low to boost supply. A new Bank of Canada (BoC) staff paper tests both claims, and neither holds up as a blanket rule. The researchers find that ignoring shelter inflation during a demand-driven boom is destabilizing to the economy and pushes valuations higher. While rate cuts get more homes built, roughly 80% of that comes from excess demand created by monetary stimulus.

Housing FOMO Makes Ignoring Shelter Inflation Risky

Can the central bank safely ignore shelter inflation? Not when demand is driving it, according to the researchers. “Monetary policy should not look through shelter inflation when it is driven by housing demand shocks. Looking through creates a more volatile economy especially when faced with extrapolative expectations,” they explain.

Extrapolative expectations is a $10 term ($184.70 in 2026 dollars) for assuming a trend will continue. Home prices rise because that’s just what they do—so buyers who believe that load up on more housing and debt during a boom.

The researchers modelled a boom where home prices climb 20% over two years. Excluding shelter inflation from policy decisions pushes overvaluation as much as 2.2 percentage points higher than a policy that includes it. When buyers have rational expectations, the gap peaks around 1.3 points. In other words, trend-chasing led to a 70% larger overshoot.

“This amplifies financial stability risks, especially when price dynamics are partly driven by past increases in house prices,” warn the researchers.

Rate Cuts Are Steroids For Demand, Not A Supply Fix

Factoring shelter into rate decisions during a boom makes a hike more likely. Higher rates cool demand over time, but they immediately raise financing costs for homebuilders. Cheaper money means more building, argues the industry. In isolation, the math makes sense. Reality is a little more complicated.

“While financing costs do affect housing supply, supply-side cost effects remain quantitatively secondary to demand-driven mechanisms operating through house prices and expectations,” explain the researchers.

They modelled a 100 basis point (bp) rate cut, which lifts residential investment 6.2%. Cheaper financing accounted for just 1.4 points of that, roughly 20%. The other 80% injection comes from excess housing demand. Rate cuts technically get more homes built, but primarily by incentivizing more housing consumption.

Mortgage Interest Makes Rate Cuts Look Like Lower Inflation

After a rate cut, shelter inflation falls for about two years. That drop is mostly mechanical, as Canada includes mortgage interest costs (MIC) in CPI. Cheaper borrowing directly lowers measured shelter inflation, even though the real impact of monetary policy decisions isn’t fully reflected for 18 to 24 months. It’s a problem most countries avoid, including the United States.

Since CPI drives rate decisions and rates drive mortgage interest costs, mortgage interest creates a feedback loop. Rates fall, mortgage interest falls, measured inflation falls, and the BoC cuts rates to lift inflation back to target. The researchers call it a “policy amplification loop,” where easing reinforces the housing boom. It makes the case for ignoring mortgage interest, even as they warn against ignoring demand-driven shelter inflation.

We’ve covered this problem in depth before, so it’s nice to see it get some time in the monetary policy spotlight.

Hiking Rates Into A Supply Shock Slows Output, Not Inflation

When a supply crunch is driving shelter inflation, hiking rates barely makes a dent. Higher rates raise mortgage interest costs, offsetting much of the cooling in home prices.

Rents rise too. In the model, rental returns have to compete with what investors could earn on financial assets, so higher rates push rents up.

Responding to shelter with hikes “does little to reduce cumulative shelter inflation,” note the researchers. Total headline inflation ends up nearly identical whether the BoC reacts to shelter or not, according to the model. Economic output is a different story.

“In contrast, reacting to the housing supply shock leads to a significantly larger decline in output. This trade-off suggests that looking through housing supply shocks may be welfare-enhancing,” the researchers conclude.

Even the case for looking through shelter inflation comes with a caveat. They warn that if the supply shock persists, the risk of de-anchoring inflation expectations rises, urging caution.

What The Bank of Canada’s Model Misses About Rates & Productivity

The researchers are clear: the BoC can’t safely ignore shelter inflation when demand is driving it, and rate cuts aren’t a supply strategy. Hikes restrain home prices even in a shortage, but measured shelter inflation barely moves, since higher mortgage interest costs and rents offset the cooling.

What the model doesn’t show is the cost to the rest of the economy. The study shows a 100 bp rate cut lifts residential investment 6.2%, dwarfing the boost to output and business investment. In this scenario of a housing demand shock, residential investment growth significantly outpaces the boost to business investment and economic output. The model treats this as a passing problem: one shock, and everything returns to normal within five years. That’s not reality.

The BoC doesn’t cut rates once, then take a decade off. Repeated easing has pushed residential investment’s growth past the rest of the economy, concentrating capital in housing. The model has no way for business investment to lift future productivity, the exact problem that policymakers are currently struggling with. It can’t count what’s lost when that capital is diverted from other industries, nor does it measure whether, when or how it returns. The paper shows where the stimulus goes. It just doesn’t capture the full cost.

items.title: Uniqlo to open first downtown location at Pacific Centre
items.description: The Japanese retailer’s seventh B.C. location will join new Aritzia and Simons flagships in the former Nordstrom space
items._ogDesc: The Japanese retailer’s seventh B.C. location will join new Aritzia and Simons flagships in the former Nordstrom space
items.body:
Uniqlo will open its first downtown Vancouver store at CF Pacific Centre in spring 2027, marking the Japanese clothing retailer’s seventh location in B.C.

The Japanese retailer will join the new Aritzia and Simons flagships to take up the space formerly occupied by Nordstrom. The three stores are scheduled to open between 2027 and 2028.

“We are incredibly proud to support the growth of Uniqlo, Simons and Aritzia across Canada with these premier locations at CF Pacific Centre,” said Lillian Tummonds, senior vice-president of retail at Cadillac Fairview, which owns and operates the shopping centre, in a statement.

“This major transformation reflects our shared commitment to creating unparalleled retail destinations, and we look forward to the energy and excitement these powerhouse brands will bring to the heart of downtown Vancouver.”

Bruce Winder, a retail analyst, said the development is a "continued vote" in downtown Vancouver retail space.

"Downtown Vancouver has had a bit of a hard time getting tenants. Recently, it's been a bit of a tough sell for some brands to sign leases," Winder said.

"And they've had to deal with ... the exit of Nordstrom. Not specifically in [Pacific Centre], but Saks Fifth Avenue have left, going back, Sears left, etc. So it's been tough to fill these large boxes."

In November 2025, Vancouver-based fashion retailer Aritzia announced plans for a four-level, 40,000-square-foot flagship boutique at CF Pacific Centre, with an opening initially targeted for 2027. Cadillac Fairview's latest announcement tentatively puts the opening in 2028.

Earlier this year, Quebec-based retailer Simons announced plans to open its first downtown Vancouver store at the shopping centre. The approximately 92,000-square-foot location will span three floors and is scheduled to open in fall 2027.

Winder said several mid-sized brands have been taking up space previously occupied by a single large retailer in downtowns across Canada, including Vancouver.

Another trend he has observed in B.C. is the rise of Asian retailers as some American chains, including Target and Nordstrom, have exited Canada, alongside the closure of Saks Off Fifth stores.

"U.S. companies seem to have a harder track record, where some of the other retailers from Asia, like Uniqlo, Miniso, Muji, and some other ones, have done better in Canada," he said.

Uniqlo opened its first Canadian store at CF Toronto Eaton Centre in 2016, followed by its first B.C. location at Metropolis at Metrotown in Burnaby in 2017.

items.body:
Expectations are rising that the Bank of Canada will indeed raise its benchmark interest rate this week as it considers the effect of higher energy prices on the economy.

Financial market odds for a rate hike were just over 83 per cent as of Monday afternoon, according to LSEG Data & Analytics. The central bank's planned interest rate announcement on Wednesday will also include an updated monetary policy report.

The Bank of Canada has held its policy rate at 2.25 per cent for seven consecutive meetings.

RBC economists said in a note to clients Thursday that they are now expecting a quarter-point hike as the central bank faces a “pivotal decision amid evolving economic conditions.”

Last week, Statistics Canada reported the annual inflation rate rose to 3.1 per cent in September as the war in the Middle East continued to drive up gasoline prices. Excluding gasoline, the consumer price index rose 2.2 per cent year-over-year in September, easing from 2.4 per cent in August, suggesting higher energy prices haven't significantly spread throughout the economy yet.

Meanwhile, jobs data from StatCan released earlier this month showed the labour market stalled for a second month in a row in September as the economy lost 68,000 positions.

However, the RBC economists said they have “very low conviction” on a rate hike happening this week, and see a significant chance the Bank of Canada instead uses the meeting to set up a hike in December or January.

"While we don’t see an immediate need for the BoC to hike now, at the same time, a 25-basis-point increase in the overnight rate on Wednesday won’t materially change our medium-term economic outlook compared to a December or January hike," the note reads.

RBC assistant chief economist Nathan Janzen said in an interview that recent comments from Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem appeared to drive the change in expectations.

While speaking from the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund meetings in Bangkok, Macklem warned that persistently high global energy prices will drive up the inflation outlook at home.

“That essentially just emphasized that the central bank is increasingly worried about the potential impact of higher oil prices on future, broader inflation pressures, and they feel confident enough the economic backdrop is going to gradually continue to improve,” Janzen said.

The Bank of Canada released its latest business outlook survey last week, which suggested that business sentiment improved on average in the third quarter. However, it found that concerns remained about rising costs and the war in the Middle East.

"All the economic data that we've had to date is consistent with the view that the central bank, the Bank of Canada, was getting closer to raising interest rates," Janzen said.

Canadian interest rates are still relatively low, he added, and the neutral range — where rates are neither helping nor hurting the economy — sits between 2.25 per cent and 3.25 per cent.

TD Bank economist Marc Ercolao said in an interview that it is clear the Bank of Canada is becoming more concerned about the persistence of rising energy prices, "and that's what's starting to change the calculus."

While a hike is likely, he said there are also arguments for the bank to hold its key rate.

"There's interest-sensitive parts of the economy, particularly housing, that are already dealing with higher bond yields and too much additional tightening risks some unnecessary weaker demand in that space," Ercolao said.

"Overall, Canada's economy is growing, but it's not necessarily overheating by any means."

The impact of U.S. trade tensions on overall investment and a weakening labour market also support a decision to hold interest rates, he said.

He said a hike on Wednesday would be a risk management measure to prevent the inflation shock from becoming more persistent.

Ercolao said higher energy prices are a double-edged sword for the domestic economy.

"On one hand, higher energy prices are good for producers and government, and corporate revenue intake. It creates higher incomes especially in commodity-producing provinces," he said.

"But at the same time, it's households especially that feel the pinch immediately from higher gasoline costs and then secondary to that, higher refined product costs end up feeding through the supply chain and into our end-user purchases."

Ercolao said that Canada has navigated the trade dispute "fairly well" by diversifying trade in certain sectors, including shipments of energy products to Asia and Europe.

"That said, there's still that acute pressure that's being placed on very reliant industries in Canada on the U.S., especially in Central Canada like Ontario and Quebec with our steel industry, our aluminum industry and our auto industry," he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 26, 2026.

Daniel Johnson, The Canadian Press
